instructions:
## The project being researched

An XGBoost "virtual sensor" for Iowa stream nitrate: predict at locations with NO physical sensor, using only weather + land-use data. Two targets:
- REGRESSION: daily-max nitrate concentration (mg/L)
- CLASSIFICATION (the primary one): binary `violation` = daily max >= 10 mg/L, base rate 0.263

~85 sensor sites, 160,074 site-days, 2008-2026. Each site has a delineated upstream drainage basin. Features are aggregated over basin cells in distance buckets from the outlet.

## THE DEPLOYMENT TARGET - judge every recommendation against this
The shipped product takes an ARBITRARY MAP PIN anywhere in Iowa, delineates its upstream basin on the fly via USGS NLDI, builds features from weather and land use alone, and predicts daily violation probability. There is NO nitrate history at the target location, NO discharge gauge there, and NO guarantee of a monitored neighbor upstream. Any method that requires the target site's own observations, or requires a gauged upstream site, DOES NOT WORK for this product - it may still be useful for other purposes, but that limitation must be stated explicitly and prominently.

## Current honest performance (leave-one-basin-family-out, LOFO)
- CLF: AUC 0.820, PR-AUC 0.634 (2.41x lift over base rate), recall 0.524 at 10% false-alarm rate, MCC 0.466, Brier 0.137
- REG: R2 0.328, RMSE 4.36 mg/L
- Deployed at beta=2: recall 0.864, but 59% of alarms are false

## THE CENTRAL PROBLEM: the model cannot rank sites
- within_r2 0.42 vs between_r2 0.21
- macro_auc 0.90 vs between_rate_r2 0.24
The project's own summary: "a good timer, a mediocre site-ranker." It captures WHEN nitrate rises at a given site, but fails at the ABSOLUTE LEVEL of an unseen basin. Essentially all remaining headroom is in the between-site term.

## CRITICAL SAMPLE-SIZE CONSTRAINT
The ~85 sites collapse to only 19 INDEPENDENT BASIN FAMILIES under the leak-safe CV (sites whose basins nest and whose records overlap in time are grouped). So learning a site's absolute level is a regression with roughly 19 effective independent units, NOT 160k rows. Any method whose published gains come from hundreds of catchments (e.g. CAMELS with 531-671 basins) must be explicitly flagged as possibly infeasible here.

## Current features (68 for CLF)
9 weather variables x 3 distance buckets (SAME-DAY SCALARS ONLY), 8 CDL crop classes x 3 buckets, 2 nitrogen-surplus x 3 buckets, doy_sin/doy_cos, 4 cross-site nitrate lags (rest_of_state_nitrate_lag1/2/3/5), 5 static (lat, lon, log_basin_area, mean_dist_to_sensor, max_dist_to_sensor).
Top features by permutation importance: rest_of_state_nitrate_lag1, lon, lat, doy_sin, fuel_moisture_1000h. BOTTOM: all daily weather; precip_in_1d is dead last (perm ~0.000).

## KNOWN NEGATIVE RESULTS - do not naively re-propose these
- Lagged weather copies: HURT badly (loso_r2 0.116 -> 0.019)
- Rolling precip / water balance as implemented: worse (lofo_r2 0.013 vs 0.003)
- Broadcasting 2017 N-surplus forward in time: much worse (-0.166)
- Rolling (3D/7D) smoothed targets: worse
- Spike / anomaly z-score targets: failed cross-site (lofo_r2 ~ -0.0006)
- Antecedent moisture + rain x surplus interactions: REG a wash, CLF only +0.017 PR-AUC
- Riparian 0-2km bucket: CLF +0.039 PR-AUC but REG worse
- Advective travel-time routing IS ALREADY IMPLEMENTED (weather per distance bucket shifted by median flow distance / 2.1 m/s) and is part of the "lagged weather hurt" failure.
PATTERN: nearly every hydrologically-motivated TEMPORAL feature has failed. The only wins came from geometry and static geography. This strongly suggests the deficit is in BETWEEN-SITE static information, not in temporal dynamics.

## Data present on disk but UNUSED
- discharge/streamflow: only 22 of 85 sites (all USGS, 0.66-0.97 density, up to 18 years). ZERO of the 61 IWQIS sites.
- co-located water chemistry: specific conductance (65 sites), water temp (80), pH (64), dissolved oxygen (64), turbidity + phosphate (61)
- upstream_uid (28 sites) / downstream_uid (40 sites) river-network topology: completely unread
- draining_area (80/85), NHDPlus comid (stored per basin), basin containment graph (used only to build CV folds)

## Known data problems
- Nitrogen surplus (gTREND product) ENDS IN 2017 -> NaN for 68% of training rows
- 16.5% of grid cells lack crop/surplus data; an inner join silently UNDER-COUNTS crop area and N surplus for basins extending outside Iowa (worst for the largest multi-state basins)
- Tile drainage density: known to be the dominant hydrologic control in Iowa, NOT in the feature set, and NO data source has been identified yet


## Non-negotiable rules for this research

1. RECORD THE SPLIT PROTOCOL FOR EVERY PERFORMANCE NUMBER, AND DO NOT COMPARE NUMBERS ACROSS PROTOCOLS. Random-split results are valid evidence about method behavior and should be reported - researchers using them often have good reasons for their own question. But only SPATIALLY HELD-OUT numbers (leave-one-basin-out, leave-one-region-out, ungauged-basin protocol) are comparable to our LOFO 0.820, because a random split over autocorrelated site-days lets a model memorize a site's level and measures interpolation rather than transfer. When the protocol cannot be determined, say so rather than guessing.
2. REPORT EFFECT SIZES AND SAMPLE SIZES, NOT CONCLUSIONS. "GNNs improve water quality prediction" is worthless. "Recurrent GCN, 456 reaches, 42 monitored, held-out-node RMSE 1.83 vs 2.11 for LSTM" is actionable. Always give the number of catchments/basins/sites used.
3. EVERY DATASET RECOMMENDATION MUST BE OPERATIONAL: exact name, spatial resolution, temporal resolution, coverage years, whether it covers ALL of Iowa AND the multi-state portions of basins, exact URL, access mechanism (API/bulk/FTP), authentication requirement, and license.
4. ACTIVELY HUNT FOR NEGATIVE RESULTS. Seven feature-engineering ablations have already failed on this project. Papers reporting that a technique did NOT transfer are as valuable as successes and are systematically under-published - look in discussion/limitations sections and in benchmark comparison papers.
5. FLAG THE n=19-FAMILIES CONSTRAINT against every recommendation. If a method's evidence base comes from 300+ basins, say so explicitly and assess whether it can work at n=19.
6. ACQUISITION CONSTRAINT: recommend only free/public data, or data obtainable by a reasonable request (e.g. emailing IIHR or Iowa DNR). No paid datasets, no field campaigns, no new sensor deployment.
7. Prefer peer-reviewed literature and authoritative agency sources over blog posts. Give DOIs where they exist.
8. JUDGE EVERYTHING AGAINST THE DEPLOYMENT TARGET: an arbitrary ungauged map pin with no local history. State plainly when a method only works at gauged sites.


## Your assignment: synthesize the findings for angle "The fluid dynamics angle: concentration-discharge behavior, dilution mass balance, and modeled streamflow"

### Research question
What does the concentration-discharge (C-Q) literature say about nitrate in agricultural catchments - chemostatic vs dilution vs mobilization behavior - and would knowing discharge at an ungauged site, obtained from a MODELED source such as the NOAA National Water Model retrospective, convert into between-site skill for concentration and exceedance prediction?

### What a good answer contains
The C-Q slope regimes for nitrate in agricultural catchments and what controls them. Whether the literature supports concentration ~ N-input-yield / specific-discharge as a BETWEEN-SITE relation, with reported R2. Concrete evaluation of NWM v3 retrospective: coverage, years, hourly/daily, access via AWS S3/Zarr, per-reach COMID join, and its KNOWN BIAS in tile-drained low-relief basins (this bias assessment is essential - modeled Q error could swamp the signal). Equivalent evaluation of alternatives: USGS SPARROW predicted mean-annual flow and N yield per reach, GAGES-II, and regionalizing streamflow from our own 22 gauged sites. Finally: whether LOAD (C x Q) is a better modeling target with concentration back-derived - that changes the target definition, not just the features. Seeds: Godsey/Kirchner power-law C-Q; Basu et al. chemostatic behavior / biogeochemical stationarity; Thompson et al.; Van Meter & Basu legacy nitrogen and transit times; Damkohler number framing (Oldham, Basu).

### TIER 3 - UNVERIFIED claims
These were extracted from real sources but were NEVER adversarially verified - verification was cut to conserve budget. The characteristic failure mode in this corpus is CONFIDENT OVERREACH FROM THIN EVIDENCE, not fabrication: a claim's conclusion is often right while its stated warrant is wrong, its effect size misattributed, or its split protocol misdescribed.

STRICT RULES for tier 3, which you MUST follow:
- USE them for COVERAGE and LEADS: naming a dataset, a URL, an access route, a candidate attribute, or an angle worth pursuing.
- DO NOT use them as the warrant for any numeric performance figure, any effect size, or the core argument of any recommendation. Those must rest on verified (tier 1) claims.
- Any finding that rests on tier 3 MUST set confidence to "unverified" and say so in the claim text itself.
- If a tier 3 claim contradicts a verified claim, the verified claim wins; note the conflict.

Produce the structured finding set for this angle as JSON.

Merge semantic duplicates. Apply every correction supplied by the verifiers. Rank findings by relevance to the BETWEEN-SITE gap specifically. For each finding give feasibilityAtN19 and worksAtUngaugedPin honestly. Populate "datasets" for every concrete data source, with howToIncorporate written concretely enough to act on - name the feature that would be created and how it would be aggregated to a basin. Populate "uncovered" for any part of the question that produced nothing verifiable - absence of evidence must be reported as absence, never silently dropped. Your "verdict" must state plainly whether this angle is worth pursuing and why.

Output JSON with keys: angle, verdict, findings[] (each: claim, confidence, effectSize, splitProtocol, nBasins, sources[], feasibilityAtN19, worksAtUngaugedPin), datasets[] (each: name, url, resolution, years, access, license, coversMultiState, whyUseful, howToIncorporate, limitations), refuted[], uncovered[].

tier1_survived.claim: The National Water Model contains NO representation of subsurface tile drainage: 'The current NWM lacks TD representation which adds considerable uncertainty to streamflow forecasts in heavily tile-drained areas' (Valayamkunnath et al. 2022, Water Resources Research, DOI 10.1029/2021WR031242). Adding a tile-drainage scheme over the heavily tile-drained Midwestern US increased simulated streamflow peaks by 14%, volume by 2.3%, and baseflow by 11%, and reduced groundwater recharge by 43-50%, surface runoff by 7-29%, and evapotranspiration by 7-13%; the scheme 'enhanced the uncalibrated NWM performance by about 20-50% of the fully calibrated NWM.' FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION FOR THIS PROJECT: NWM v2.1/v3.0 retrospective streamflow in Iowa carries a STRUCTURAL, SPATIALLY SYSTEMATIC low bias whose magnitude scales with tile density — i.e. the error is correlated with the exact basin property that controls nitrate. This is the worst possible error structure for a between-site feature: it will not average out across the 19 families, and modeled-Q error could plausibly swamp the between-site signal it is meant to supply. SOURCE CAVEAT: full text paywalled; abstract retrieved verbatim via Semantic Scholar. Per-gauge NSE/KGE tables and the number of gauges evaluated were NOT retrievable and are recorded as unknown.
tier1_survived.effectSize: tile drainage changes NWM peaks +14%, volume +2.3%, baseflow +11%, recharge -43 to -50%; TD scheme recovers 20-50% of the gap between uncalibrated and calibrated NWM
corrections:
The claim itself is accurate and should stand. Two corrections to how it is being used, plus one actionable finding.

1. The FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION overstates what the paper supports. The paper's own headline result — the TD scheme "enhanced the UNCALIBRATED NWM performance by about 20-50% of the fully calibrated NWM" — means calibration alone already recovers roughly half to four-fifths of what the missing tile-drainage process costs. The operational NWM v2.1/v3.0 retrospectives are calibrated products with regionalized parameters, i.e. the Calib/CalibTD arm of the paper, not the Uncalib arm. The paper shows CalibTD beats Calib, so residual structural error exists, but its magnitude in the calibrated configuration is not the 14%/11%/2.3% numbers — those are TD-on-vs-TD-off simulation deltas, and the volume delta is only 2.3%. Correct statement: "Calibrated NWM in tile-drained regions absorbs the missing tile-drainage process into distorted parameter values rather than leaving a clean unmitigated low bias; a residual, plausibly tile-density-correlated error remains, of unquantified magnitude in the calibrated retrospective."

2. The sign is not established as a uniform "low bias." Adding TD increased peaks and baseflow but DECREASED surface runoff (−7 to −29%) and recharge (−43 to −50%); the redistribution is between flow pathways, with net volume changing only 2.3%. The no-TD NWM is therefore mis-partitioned rather than simply low. Since nitrate delivery in Iowa is dominated by the tile pathway specifically, a mis-partitioned NWM Q is arguably a worse feature than a uniformly biased one — the caution in the claim is directionally right, but the mechanism should be stated as pathway mis-partitioning, not low bias.

3. ACTIONABLE, AND MORE VALUABLE THAN THE CLAIM ITSELF: the same first author published the tile-drainage dataset this project lists as an unfilled gap ("NO data source has been identified yet"). Valayamkunnath, Barlage, Chen, Gochis, Franz (2020), "Mapping of 30-meter resolution tile-drained croplands using a geospatial modeling approach," Scientific Data 7:257, DOI 10.1038/s41597-020-00596-x, open access CC BY. Dataset AgTile-US: 30 m binary raster (1 = tile-drained cropland, 0 = undrained), CONUS-wide (so it covers the multi-state portions of the large basins, not just Iowa), static representation for base year 2017 (built from USDA NASS 2017 Census of Agriculture county tile acreage + SSURGO drainage class + SRTM slope + NLCD 2016 crop mask). Overall accuracy 86.03% against 16,000 ground-truth points; IOWA SPECIFICALLY 91.1% accuracy on 5,253 ground-truth points; heavily tile-drained Midwest states 82.7-93.6%. Access: figshare DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.11825742, no login, no authentication — verified via the figshare v2 API, license CC BY 4.0, files AgTile-US-TIFF.zip (125.8 MB), AgTile-US-NetCDF.zip (128.9 MB), AgTile-US.zip (185.2 MB), plus a metadata txt. Direct download e.g. https://ndownloader.figshare.com/files/23079140.

Fit to the deployment target: this is a STATIC RASTER, so tile-drained fraction can be computed for an arbitrary NLDI-delineated basin at a map pin with zero local history and zero gauge — it satisfies the deployment constraint completely, unlike modeled NWM discharge. It is exactly the class of feature that has historically worked on this project (static geography and geometry) and not the class that has failed seven times (temporal/hydrologic). Caveats to flag: (a) n=19 families still applies — tile fraction per basin is one number per site, so it adds at most a couple of degrees of freedom to the between-site term and cannot be validated as a "win" on 19 units without wide error bars; (b) it is static for 2017, so it carries no time variation and cannot be broadcast as a time-varying feature (recall the 2017 N-surplus broadcast failure — use it as a static basin attribute only, never expanded per-day as a pseudo-temporal variable); (c) it is a modeled product constrained to county census totals, so within-county spatial detail is a decision-tree allocation, not observation, and its errors are spatially structured by county boundary; (d) the crop mask is NLCD 2016, which the authors report has 18% less cropland than the USDA census, so tile area is under-allocated in some counties.

Bottom line on the original claim's practical advice: the caution against using NWM modeled discharge as a between-site feature is reasonable but rests on an over-strong reading of the abstract. The far stronger move implied by the same author's work is to skip modeled Q entirely and ingest AgTile-US tile fraction per distance bucket as a static basin attribute.

The cited source says exactly what the claim quotes — every quoted phrase and every percentage is verbatim-correct — so the attribution stands. Three corrections are required.

(1) The unknowns are now known, and they weaken the claim's leverage: NWM **V2.0** (not v2.1/v3.0); **49 calibration basins** (>=10% tile area, 10-20,000 km2) and **139 USGS gauges** for regional evaluation, from a 188-gauge pool; protocol is a **temporal split on the same basins** (calibrate WY2008-2013, evaluate Oct 2013-Oct 2019), NOT leave-one-basin-out. Spatial transfer appears only as Gower's-distance parameter regionalization from the 49 donors to 939 HUC10 receivers, which is itself never independently validated. The "20-50%" figure is a median-of-seasonal-distributions statement on the 49 calibration basins.

(2) The falsifiable implication is NOT supported by this source and is partly contradicted. The +14%/+2.3%/+11% numbers are a TD-on vs TD-off sensitivity **within a single calibrated parameter set** ("No tile drainage ... is not equal to Calib"), not a bias of any operational NWM run. Because the operational NWM is calibrated, the missing tile process is largely absorbed into compensated parameters — the paper says Calib's DKSAT is "an effective hydraulic conductivity for the combined subsurface material and tile drain system" and that Calib is "over-calibrated to accommodate the absence of TD". The residual bias is not a uniform low bias: against 139 gauges, Calib's median event peak-flow bias is **+5% (high)**, and low flows are **overestimated** (CalibTD still +50%). Most decisively, the paper **never regresses bias against tile-drainage percentage**, so "error magnitude scales with tile density" is an untested extrapolation, not a finding. Rewrite the claim as: NWM V2.0 omits tile drainage, and switching the process on changes simulated Midwest hydrology substantially; the resulting error in the *calibrated* operational product is seasonally and flow-regime dependent (high-flow peaks slightly over, low flows strongly over), and its correlation with tile density is unquantified in the literature.

(3) The practical consequence for this project is the opposite of the claim's framing. The paper is not a reason to avoid modeled Q; it is the origin of the tile-drainage dataset the project has been unable to find. **AgTile-US** — 30 m binary tile-drained cropland, CONUS coverage including the out-of-Iowa parts of multi-state basins, static single epoch, figshare DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.11825742, CC BY 4.0, unauthenticated bulk download (TIFF 126 MB / NetCDF 129 MB), described in Sci Data 7:257 DOI 10.1038/s41597-020-00596-x — is directly ingestible as percent-tile-drained per distance bucket. It is a static between-site geographic feature, the only feature family that has produced wins here, and it requires no discharge record at the target pin. Recommend it as a first-class action item; treat NWM retrospective Q as a separate, lower-priority and more error-prone proposition.

Keep the source-level claim; discard or heavily qualify the derived implication. Four corrections, in order of importance to this project:

1. THE BIAS DIRECTION IS WRONG. The implication asserts NWM carries a "structural, spatially systematic LOW bias" in tile-drained Iowa. The paper's own bias statistics say the opposite for the operational (calibrated) configuration: median event PEAK-FLOW BIAS in Calib is +5% (over-prediction), reduced to +0.57% in CalibTD; the median low-flow bias in Calib is TWICE that of Default, and even CalibTD "still overestimated low flows by 50%." The paper attributes low-flow over-prediction to excessive groundwater recharge and the one-way NWM groundwater scheme (citing Jachens et al. 2021; Karki et al. 2021). Operational NWM in tile country reads as biased HIGH at low flow and mildly high at peaks, not low.

2. THE +14%/+2.3%/+11% ARE MODEL-MINUS-MODEL SENSITIVITIES, NOT MEASURED BIASES AGAINST OBSERVATIONS. They come from "comparing 'No tile drainage' with 'With tile drainage'" simulations (Sec. 3.4), i.e. CalibTD vs Calib. Critically, when TD is added WITHOUT recalibration the level does not move: "There are no considerable differences in the estimated Bias between Default and DefaultTD" and "There is no considerable difference between Default and DefaultTD in the estimated peak flow bias." What TD buys is DYNAMICS and TIMING — COR +0.15, NSE +0.16, KGE +0.22 for high flows (DefaultTD vs Default); event hit rate 44%→~65% (Default→DefaultTD), 78% in CalibTD vs 71% in Calib; false-alarm rate 22.5%→17.5%; peak timing error −3/0/4/2 h. The 20–50% figure is likewise an improvement in NSE/KGE-type skill (e.g. spring median NSE 0.22→0.33 for DefaultTD vs 0.22→0.55 for Calib), not a bias correction.

3. THE PAPER NEVER TESTS ERROR-VS-TILE-DENSITY SCALING, AND ITS DESIGN CANNOT. Both gauge sets are pre-screened to tile fraction ≥10% (49 calibration basins and the 188-gauge pool), truncating the range of the exact covariate the implication needs. No regression or stratification of NWM error against tile fraction appears anywhere in the paper. The paper's actual closing mechanism runs the other way for level: "the operational NWM parameters are over-calibrated to accommodate the absence of the TD process in the model during winter and spring" — i.e. operational calibration has already absorbed much of the missing-TD water-balance effect into parameter values, which makes residual level error idiosyncratic-per-donor-basin rather than a clean monotone function of tile density. That is a weaker and messier error structure than the claim asserts, but it is still bad for a between-site feature — just for a different reason (regionalization-donor artifacts, not tile-scaled low bias).

4. VERSION AND MAGNITUDE SCOPE. The study is NWM V2.0; it says nothing about v2.1 or v3.0 retrospective, so "v2.1/v3.0 carries this bias" is an extrapolation, not a finding (that these versions still lack a tile scheme is plausible but must be verified separately against NWM release documentation, not this DOI). And the alarming −43% to −50% figure is GROUNDWATER RECHARGE, an internal flux absent from the streamflow product; the streamflow-volume effect is 2.3% annually (seasonal 17% winter / 13% spring / 13% fall / 2.8% summer). The risk to a modeled-Q feature is real at event/peak scale, small at annual-volume scale.

PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE FOR THIS PROJECT (deployment target: arbitrary ungauged Iowa map pin). Do not use this paper to rule out NWM retrospective Q as a feature; it does not establish the tile-scaled low bias the argument needs. But also do not expect NWM Q to fix the between-site deficit: everything the paper demonstrates TD improves — timing, hit rate, event dynamics — is the axis on which this model is already strong ("a good timer"), and the paper shows the LEVEL effect gets absorbed by calibration. Prior expectation for NWM Q as a between-site level feature should therefore be LOW, on the paper's own evidence.

CHEAP DIRECT TEST THAT DOMINATES FURTHER LITERATURE SEARCH: the project already has observed discharge at 22 USGS sites. Pull NWM v3.0 retrospective Q (CONUS, hourly, 1979–2023, NHDPlusV2 comid-indexed — comids are already stored per basin; free, no auth, Zarr/NetCDF on the NOAA Open Data Dissemination AWS bucket noaa-nwm-retrospective-3-0-pds, s3://noaa-nwm-retrospective-3-0-pds, public domain) and regress NWM-vs-observed percent bias on AgTile-US tile fraction across those 22. That measures the error structure directly in Iowa instead of inferring it, and it needs no new data acquisition. AgTile-US itself (30 m binary tile-drained cropland, CONUS, one epoch ~2017, Valayamkunnath, Barlage, Chen, Gochis, Franz 2020, Scientific Data, DOI 10.1038/s41597-020-00596-x, free download) is separately the most concrete answer to the project's flagged "no tile-drainage data source identified" gap — note its CONUS extent covers the multi-state portions of the large basins, which is exactly where the current Iowa-only crop/N-surplus inner join under-counts.

n=19 CAVEAT: this source's n (49 calibration basins, 139 evaluation gauges, 939 HUC10s) is not a constraint on using its FINDING, since the finding is about a physical model's structure, not a learned mapping. The n=19 constraint bites only on the downstream test above, where 22 gauged sites give weak power to detect a bias-vs-tile-density slope — expect to be able to rule out only large effects.

Towler et al. 2023 (HESS 27:1809) is correctly cited as to study, n=5,390 USGS gauges, period 1983-2016, region definition (Falcone aggregated ecoregions, not HUC2), metric (KGE, not NSE), and the direction of the result (Central is the worst region; NWMv2.1 exceeds NHMv1.0 by ~0.08-0.10 KGE). Towler et al. 2023 (HESS 27:1809, DOI 10.5194/hess-27-1809-2023) benchmarked NWMv2.1 and NHMv1.0 daily streamflow against 5,390 USGS gauges, 1 Oct 1983 - 31 Dec 2016 (~33 yr, ~12,100 d). Critically for Iowa: the "plains" sentence names North Dakota, South Dakota, Nebraska, Kansas, and Texas. Chemostasis predicts that adding Q would mainly improve LOAD (C x Q) prediction while leaving concentration and the 10 mg/L exceedance target largely unimproved. This is directly testable on the 22 already-gauged sites BEFORE any NWM ingestion: compute CVc/CVq per site from existing nitrate + USGS discharge; if the median is well below 1, the fluid-dynamics angle is predicted to fail for the concentration target and load-as-target is predicted NOT to help concentration back-derivation. SOURCE CAVEAT: full text paywalled (HTTP 402); abstract retrieved via Semantic Scholar. Exact site count, drainage-area range, power-law slope b values, and CVc/CVq figures were NOT retrievable.

corrections:
The citation is accurate — the quoted clause "tile drainage is a dominant control on C-Q dynamics, with increasing drainage density contributing to more chemostatic C-Q behavior" is verbatim from the abstract of Marinos, Van Meter & Basu (2020), GRL, DOI 10.1029/2020GL087051. Two details to fix: (a) the paper says "six orders of magnitude" of basin size, not "multiple orders"; (b) the paper reports a piecewise/threshold power law (per a 2025 citing paper), not a single global slope b, and no b, CVc/CVq, or site-count values are retrievable — the article is closed access (Unpaywall: oa_status "closed", zero OA locations, no repository copy), so no numeric threshold may be attributed to it.

The FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION, however, does not follow and should be rewritten. Three corrections:

1. The paper does NOT support a blanket "Iowa nitrate is largely chemostatic" premise. Its second finding is that CVc/CVq RISES with basin size, so chemostasis is a property of small, tile-dense headwaters and erodes toward the large multi-state basins. The project's proposed test on 22 USGS-gauged sites samples the large-basin end preferentially — the least chemostatic end — so its median CVc/CVq is an upper bound and is not generalizable to the small ungauged basins a map pin will often produce. Stratify any such test by drainage area rather than reporting a single median.

2. "Chemostatic ⇒ Q is uninformative about concentration" is a non-sequitur. CVc/CVq << 1 constrains a variance ratio, not a correlation, and the operative target is a 10 mg/L threshold with a 0.263 base rate — a low-amplitude but well-correlated Q signal can still flip exceedance for sites whose level sits near the threshold. The defensible prediction is narrower: chemostasis predicts Q will add little to concentration R2 while possibly still helping the binary violation target near the threshold, and predicts that load (C x Q) is close to a linear function of Q and therefore adds little independent information beyond Q itself.

3. The actionable content of this paper for this project is the OPPOSITE of "drop the fluid-dynamics angle." Chemostasis means C ≈ a site-level constant, which is exactly the between-site term the model fails (between_r2 0.21). The paper identifies TILE DRAINAGE DENSITY as a dominant control on that regime — i.e., it is external, geographically on-target (Upper Mississippi Basin) evidence that the project's single known missing static feature is first-order. As a static per-basin covariate it costs one degree of freedom and is compatible with the n=19-families constraint and with ungauged deployment, unlike per-site level learning. Caveat: the paper's "high-resolution nitrate" data may be the same IIHR/IWQIS + USGS sensor network this project trains on, in which case it is a prior analysis of our own data rather than independent corroboration; obtain the full text to check before citing it as external validation.

The quoted sentence is verbatim-accurate from the abstract of Marinos, Van Meter & Basu (2020) GRL 10.1029/2020GL087051 ("Is the River a Chemostat?..."), so the citation itself stands. Three corrections to how it is being used:

1. SCALE FINDING IS BEING READ BACKWARDS. The paper says CVc/CVq INCREASES with basin size across SIX orders of magnitude — i.e. larger basins are MORE chemodynamic. Iowa's ~85 monitored sites sit at the larger end of that gradient, so the paper predicts nitrate at our sites is chemoDYNAMIC, not chemostatic. The "more chemostatic" phrase is a relative, comparative statement about high-tile-density vs low-tile-density catchments, not an absolute b≈0 claim, and no CVc/CVq or b value is retrievable from any accessible source (paper is closed-access, Unpaywall oa_locations empty, no repository copy, no preprint). The claim's threshold rule ("median well below 1") is invented, not sourced.

2. THE PAPER FIT THRESHOLD C-Q MODELS, NOT FLAT ONES. Citing papers state Marinos et al. used a piecewise power law with fitted breakpoint Qt (b1, b2, Qt), and the paper is routinely cited as a canonical source for BREAKPOINTS and nonlinearity in nitrate C-Q. A separate UMRB study cites it as evidence that "nitrate exhibited consistently chemodynamic behavior." So the paper cannot be used to predict that discharge carries little information about concentration; if anything it implies a threshold/mobilization response that a monotone linear Q feature would miss but a tree model like XGBoost is well suited to capture.

3. THE INFERENCE "CHEMOSTASIS => Q USELESS FOR CONCENTRATION" IS A CATEGORY ERROR FOR THIS PROJECT. Chemostasis is a within-site C-Q slope statement; our headroom is between-site (within_r2 0.42 vs between_r2 0.21). Under chemostasis a site's absolute concentration level is set by static source strength — which makes the paper's FIRST finding (tile drainage density is a dominant control) the actionable one: it is a static, between-site, ungauged-transferable covariate, exactly the class of feature that has worked on this project (lat/lon/geometry) while every temporal-hydrology feature has failed. Marinos et al. is therefore evidence FOR prioritizing a tile-drainage-density layer over NWM discharge ingestion, but NOT evidence that discharge will fail.

METHODOLOGICAL LIMITS TO STATE WHENEVER THIS IS CITED: n=33 watersheds (per citing papers; not verifiable in the closed full text), UMRB, >1 year of high-frequency (5-15 min to daily-mean) nitrate sensor data. Purely descriptive/correlative — NO split protocol, no held-out prediction, so it is not comparable to and says nothing directly about our LOFO 0.820. n=33 is in the same order as our 19 families, so it is not a 500-basin result that cannot transfer; but its site set spans six orders of magnitude in area within one basin, so nested-catchment pseudoreplication in the CVc/CVq-vs-area regression is plausible and undetermined. Every C-Q metric it reports requires the site's OWN nitrate AND discharge record, so nothing in this paper is directly computable at an arbitrary ungauged map pin — its only deployable output for us is the qualitative ranking of tile density as a between-site control.

The proposed diagnostic (compute CVc/CVq on the 22 USGS-gauged sites before any NWM ingestion) is still worth running — it is cheap and it is the right descriptive statistic — but the decision rule attached to it is wrong on two counts: (a) the paper predicts CVc/CVq > 1 (chemodynamic) at our basin sizes, so a low median would CONTRADICT rather than confirm the paper; and (b) whatever CVc/CVq comes out, it is a within-site statistic and cannot adjudicate the between-site deficit that holds essentially all remaining headroom. Do not use it to kill the discharge feature; use it to decide whether Q enters as a threshold/percentile-of-local-flow-regime feature rather than a raw magnitude.

The cited finding is quoted VERBATIM and correctly attributed — do not treat Marinos, Van Meter & Basu (2020) as misused. Both abstract sentences appear word-for-word in the claim, and I independently REPLICATED the scale finding on this project's own data (Spearman(drainage area, CVc/CVq) = +0.688 across 18 gauged sites spanning 17–12,483 km²).

What IS wrong is the FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION, and it is wrong at its logical core, not in detail. Three corrections:

1. THE PROPOSED TEST WAS RUN AND ITS DECISION RULE FAILS. Median CVc/CVq = 0.443 on the 20 usable gauged sites — "well below 1", which by the claim's own stated criterion predicts "the fluid-dynamics angle will fail". Yet at those same sites, log Q explains a MEDIAN 50.9% of the variance in log nitrate concentration (per-site R² range 0.21–0.87), with median power-law slope b = +0.61. A slope of +0.61 is strongly MOBILIZING/enriching, not chemostatic (chemostasis is b ≈ 0). CVc/CVq is low here because CVq is large (median 1.4), not because C is insensitive to Q. CVc/CVq is a variance-ratio, not a mutual-information measure; it conflates "C is buffered" with "Q is wild". The test as specified cannot license the conclusion drawn from it.

2. "IOWA NITRATE IS LARGELY CHEMOSTATIC" IS NOT WHAT THE PAPER SAYS. The abstract asserts a GRADIENT ("increasing drainage density contributing to MORE chemostatic behavior") — a comparative statement — plus the finding that chemostasis WEAKENS with basin size. Iowa's monitored network is dominated by mid-to-large basins, exactly the regime the paper says is LEAST chemostatic. The claim's premise therefore inverts the paper's own scale result when applied to this network.

3. THE 10 mg/L TARGET IS WHERE Q IS MOST INFORMATIVE, NOT LEAST. At the highest-exceedance gauged sites the C-Q coupling is strongest: USGS-05481000 (55.2% violation-days) b=0.75, R²=0.63; USGS-05482500 (37.1%) b=0.73, R²=0.50; USGS-05451210 (33.0%) b=0.90, R²=0.87. The prediction that Q would help load but not exceedance is contradicted at precisely the sites that carry the exceedance signal.

CAVEATS THAT STILL FAVOR CAUTION ON Q — but for reasons unrelated to chemostasis, and these must be stated instead of the chemostasis argument: (a) the 50.9% R² is a WITHIN-SITE, non-spatially-held-out diagnostic; it speaks to the within_r2=0.42 timing term the model ALREADY handles, not the between-site absolute-level term where all the headroom is; (b) it requires OBSERVED Q at the site, which the deployment target (arbitrary ungauged map pin) does not have — modelled Q (NWM) is largely a deterministic function of the same weather + basin geometry already in the feature set, so its marginal information may be far below 50%; (c) only USGS sites have Q, so all 61 IWQIS sites — smaller, higher tile-drainage density, i.e. the MOST chemostatic per the paper — are untested here, and the true statewide median CVc/CVq is likely lower than 0.443; (d) 20 sites collapse to ≈19 independent basin families, so the per-site medians rest on very few effective units.

UNVERIFIABLE: the paper's site count, drainage-area range, b values, and CVc/CVq magnitudes remain unretrievable. Unpaywall, OpenAlex, and Semantic Scholar all report is_oa=false with zero OA locations; agupubs returns HTTP 402. The claim's own SOURCE CAVEAT is accurate and should be carried into the report verbatim. "Six orders of magnitude" is the only quantitative figure that can be sourced.

tier1_survived.claim: The standard quantitative criterion for chemostatic solute behavior is CVc/CVq << 1, with CVc/CVq < 0.3 conventionally taken as the chemostatic threshold, where CVc and CVq are the coefficients of variation of concentration and discharge (metric proposed by Thompson et al. 2011, Water Resources Research, DOI 10.1029/2010WR009605). Basu et al. (2010) separately used the r-squared of the linear regression between ANNUAL load and ANNUAL discharge as a chemostasis measure, implying linearity in the load-Q relation; chemostatic responses in agricultural catchments are attributed to a large legacy soil/groundwater N store buffering concentration, and homogeneously distributed sources produce chemostatic export while heterogeneously distributed sources produce chemodynamic export. FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION: this gives a concrete, cheap decision rule computable on the project's own 22 gauged sites with data already on disk. It also predicts the sign of the between-site relation: under chemostasis the site-mean concentration should track the N-source term (surplus, row-crop fraction, tile density) rather than the hydrologic term, which is consistent with this project's observed pattern that static geography features win and every temporal hydrologic feature has failed.
tier1_survived.effectSize: CVc/CVq < 0.3 = chemostatic; CVc/CVq near or above 1 = chemodynamic
corrections: Salvageable, corrected version: (1) CVc/CVq << 1 is a real and standard chemostasis criterion, and Thompson et al. 2011 (WRR, DOI 10.1029/2010WR009605) is a correct co-attribution alongside Musolff et al. 2015 (Adv. Water Resour. 86, 133-146). (2) The threshold is NOT 0.3. Use 0.5 (the value Frietsch & Schuetz 2026, Musolff et al. 2017 and Ebeling et al. 2021 adopt following Thompson et al. 2011) or 1.0 (Musolff et al. 2015), and state which. Thompson et al. 2011 did not itself publish a hard cutoff. (3) Basu et al. 2010 (GRL, DOI 10.1029/2010GL045168) is correctly described as using zero-intercept linear annual-load-vs-annual-discharge regression, R2 = 0.7 +/- 0.2, on 21 MARB + 14 BSDB large catchments — but it explicitly reports that TN and TP in the MARB are NON-chemostatic at daily and monthly timescales, which is this project's timescale and region. Chemostasis here is an annual, 10^4-10^6 km2 statement and must not be imported to daily 10 mg/L exceedance. (4) The homogeneous-source-to-chemostasis link is real but incomplete: Thompson et al. require BOTH spatial uniformity of the mass store AND sufficient inter-event time for mass-transfer equilibrium; Musolff et al. 2017 (DOI 10.1002/2017GL072630) adds heterogeneity in travel times as a co-driver. (5) Drop the between-site inference entirely as stated, and invert it into the actually useful and testable form: under chemostasis, site-mean concentration approximates long-term N mass flux divided by long-term water yield, so the correct between-site predictor is N surplus (or row-crop fraction, or tile density) NORMALIZED BY long-term mean runoff or precipitation climatology. The project currently has same-day weather scalars only and no static climatological water-yield term; adding a 30-year mean annual runoff/precipitation basin average as a STATIC feature is the recommendation this theory actually supports, and unlike CVc/CVq it is computable at an arbitrary ungauged map pin (e.g. from PRISM 30-yr normals or a gridded runoff climatology). (6) Treat CVc/CVq itself as a within-site diagnostic on the 22 gauged sites only, report it stratified by basin area because Marinos et al. 2020 (GRL, DOI 10.1029/2020GL087051) show it rises systematically with basin size across six orders of magnitude in the Upper Mississippi and falls with tile drainage density, and do not use it as a model feature, since the deployment target has no discharge record.

The claim is substantively correct on attribution and mechanism but wrong on its one load-bearing number, and overstates what the metric delivers. Precise corrections:

(1) THRESHOLD: replace "CVc/CVq < 0.3" with the two thresholds actually used in the literature: CVc/CVq <= 0.5 (chemostatic) vs > 0.5 (chemodynamic), cited to Thompson et al. 2011 by users such as egusphere-2025-1588; OR CVc/CVq < 1, cited to Musolff et al. 2015 (Advances in Water Resources 86, DOI 10.1016/j.advwatres.2015.09.026). No published source uses 0.3. Both thresholds are conventions tuned to particular datasets, not physical constants -- one paper states plainly it chose 0.5 because it "provides a clear separation of solute groups in our dataset."

(2) ATTRIBUTION: attribution of CVc/CVq to Thompson et al. 2011 is defensible but not uniquely correct; the Speir/Rose 2023 WIREs Water review credits Musolff et al. 2015. Cite both.

(3) BASU 2010 DETAIL: the annual load vs annual discharge linearity framing is consistent with the abstract, but the specific claim that they used the r-squared of that regression as the chemostasis measure is UNVERIFIED. Do not quote it as established.

(4) SCALE CONFOUND (must be added): CVc/CVq rises systematically with basin area across six orders of magnitude (Marinos, Van Meter & Basu 2020, GRL, "Is the river a chemostat?"). A fixed cutoff applied across the project's 22 gauged sites will partly sort them by size, not regime. Any use of CVc/CVq here must control for log_basin_area or it risks reproducing a feature already in the model.

(5) SCOPE (must be added): CVc/CVq requires both C and Q at the site. It is computable on only 22 of 85 sites (all USGS; zero IWQIS, confirmed in data_inventory.md) and is NEVER computable at the deployment target -- an arbitrary ungauged map pin. It is a hypothesis diagnostic, not a candidate feature.

(6) THE BETWEEN-SITE INFERENCE IS NOT ENTAILED: CVc/CVq is a within-site temporal statistic and does not predict the sign or strength of the between-site relation between mean concentration and N-source terms. The legacy-store narrative motivates that expectation; the metric does not test it. Confirming low CVc/CVq on the gauged subset would be consistent with the project's observed pattern (static geography wins, temporal hydrology fails) but would add no new between-site information and would not close the between_r2 = 0.21 gap. Testing the actual between-site hypothesis requires regressing site-mean concentration on source terms across sites -- n~19 independent families, underpowered, and confounded by basin area.

The citation checks out and the numbers are exact — keep it — but three things must be fixed before this is used to justify anything.

1. PROVENANCE OF THE 0.3. It is not a "conventional" threshold. It is 0.17 + 2 x 0.06, two SDs above the mean CVc/CVq of GEOGENIC solutes measured at Thompson's own 31 subwatersheds (nested in 9 experimental sites, 0.1-22 km2). It is a relative reference calibrated on that dataset, in a paper with only 2 agricultural catchments. Do not cite it as a community standard, and do not treat crossing 0.3 as a physical fact about an Iowa basin. Also fix the title ("across impact gradients") and drop "chemodynamic" — the word never appears; CVc/CVq = 1 is Godsey et al. 2009's pure-DILUTION null (C ~ 1/Q), not a chemodynamic label.

2. THE PAPER DOES NOT ESTABLISH THAT AGRICULTURAL NITRATE IS CHEMOSTATIC. Its nitrate result is mean CVc/CVq = 0.70 (SD 0.49) — above the 0.3 line for most sites — with only the sparse high-export tail reaching 0.2-0.4, and the abstract explicitly says "further data are needed to confirm its generality." The agricultural-legacy-N story rests on Basu et al. 2010 GRL (doi:10.1029/2010GL045168), which is ANNUAL total-N load vs ANNUAL discharge over MARB and Baltic basins, not daily concentration. Cite Basu for the legacy-N mechanism, not Thompson.

3. THE FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION AS STATED IS NOT WHAT CHEMOSTASIS PREDICTS. Chemostasis constrains WITHIN-site variance of C relative to Q. It does not say the between-site mean concentration tracks the source term alone. Under Basu's own formulation the invariant quantity is the flow-weighted concentration Cf = LT/QT — a RATIO. So chemostasis predicts site-mean concentration ~ (delivered N load per unit area) / (mean annual runoff depth), which means the hydrologic term does not drop out, it moves into the DENOMINATOR as a long-term water-yield normalizer. That is a genuinely different and more useful engineering prescription than "use surplus and row-crop fraction": build a static per-basin feature of the form (N surplus or row-crop fraction) / (long-term mean annual runoff or precipitation), i.e. a normalized source-loading intensity, rather than the raw source terms currently in the model. This is a static, climatological feature computable at an arbitrary ungauged pin from PRISM/Daymet normals plus a runoff-coefficient raster — it does not need the target's discharge. That is the actionable, deployment-compatible reading, and it is not what the claim states.

Two further constraints to attach. (a) DIAGNOSTIC ONLY, NEVER A FEATURE: CVc/CVq needs paired C and Q at the site. That exists at 22 of 85 sites (26%, all USGS, zero IWQIS) and at ZERO arbitrary map pins. It can characterize the training sites; it can never be an input at deployment. (b) THE n CONSTRAINT BITES TWICE: those 22 gauged sites collapse to well under 19 independent basin families, so any regression of site-mean level on chemostasis-derived predictors has single-digit effective units — smaller than Thompson's own 9 independent sites, and with the same nesting problem. Additionally the timescale is wrong for the product: CVc/CVq is a whole-distribution variance statistic computed on daily-to-monthly grab samples (Basu's on annual aggregates), while the target is DAILY-MAX nitrate crossing 10 mg/L. A basin can be perfectly chemostatic at CVc/CVq = 0.3 and still swing across 10 mg/L constantly if its mean sits near 8. Chemostasis says nothing about the upper tail, which is the entire classification problem.

Finally, "consistent with our observed pattern that static geography wins and temporal features fail" is post-hoc, not diagnostic. A chemodynamic system with uninformative same-day weather features would produce the identical symptom, and the failed features were precipitation and fuel moisture, not discharge — the C-Q relation was never actually tested here. If you want a real test, compute CVc/CVq on the 22 gauged sites (checking, as Thompson does in para [23], that the flow range during concentration sampling spans the full flow-duration curve, and noting the 0.66-0.97 discharge density gaps), and separately regress site-mean nitrate on surplus/runoff. The CV ratio itself decides nothing about the model.

OPERATIONAL FIT: CONUS-wide coverage means it covers the multi-state portions of the largest basins, which is exactly where the project's existing inner-join under-counting is worst. It is a SINGLE-EPOCH STATIC layer (2017 census basis), so it must be used as a time-invariant per-basin covariate — it CANNOT be broadcast as a time-varying feature, which is the failure mode that produced this project's -0.166 result when 2017 N-surplus was broadcast forward. corrections:
Claim is accurate as written; adopt it, but state these five caveats explicitly when using the layer.

(a) "86.03% accuracy" is RECALL ON POSITIVES ONLY — there is no false-positive assessment. All 16,000 points were manually digitized from ESRI aerial imagery at locations "when a tile drainage signature is detected," i.e. all are tile-present positives. The paper's own arithmetic confirms this: 86.03% accuracy + "13.97% omission error" = 100%. There is no confusion matrix, no true negatives, no commission error, no kappa. A map that over-painted tile everywhere would score ~100% under this validation. This matters directly for us: we intend a basin-MEAN fraction, and mean fraction is biased precisely by commission error, which is the one error mode never measured. Do not describe this as "86% classification accuracy" in project docs; describe it as "86.03% of known tile-drained ground-truth points correctly captured (omission error only; commission error unquantified)."

(b) Validation is not fully independent of model fitting. The paper extracts the slope thresholds that constrain the decision tree from the same ground-truth point set later used for validation. Treat 86.03%/91.1% as optimistic in-sample-flavored numbers.

(c) The map is CENSUS-CONSTRAINED BY COUNTY by construction — cells are accumulated until the county total matches the 2017 USDA census. So county aggregates reproduce the census almost exactly, and the map's genuine added value is sub-county ALLOCATION. For a basin spanning several counties, basin-mean tile fraction is close to an area-weighted county-census average. Effective independent information is ~county-scale (99 counties in Iowa), not 30 m. Still fine at n=19 families, but do not claim 30 m of real signal.

(d) Known systematic low bias, stated by the authors: NLCD-2016 underrepresents cropland by "18.15% underrepresentation for the CONUS," and average USDA census error is "19.8%." Tile fraction is therefore biased low, unevenly.

(e) Denominator ambiguity — a practical implementation note. Because non-cropland cells are 0, a naive basin-mean conflates "not tiled" with "not cropland." Compute BOTH tile_area/basin_area and tile_area/cropland_area per distance bucket; the latter is the actual management-intensity signal and the former is the loading-relevant one.

Finally, one risk to the falsifiable prediction that the claim should have flagged: tile-drained fraction is spatially very smooth across Iowa (Des Moines Lobe vs. Loess Hills / driftless SE), and lon and lat are already the #2 and #3 permutation-importance features. There is a real chance XGBoost has already absorbed most of this signal through lat/lon and the new columns add little. That does not argue against trying it — it is cheap, static, and of the exact class that has produced this project's only wins — but the ablation should be run against a lat/lon-included baseline (not a stripped one), and a null result should be interpreted as "already captured by coordinates," not as "tile drainage does not matter."

The claim is substantively correct and I could not refute it — quoted numbers are verbatim, the citation, DOI, input datasets, resolution, single-epoch status, license, and unauthenticated figshare download all verify (download confirmed by ranged GET returning a valid zip). Five corrections of detail:

1. "86.03% accuracy" is NOT balanced two-class accuracy. The paper pairs it with "omission error of 13.97%" (summing to 100), so it is producer's accuracy/recall on tile-drained points only. Commission error, class balance, precision and kappa are never reported — the layer's false-positive rate is unquantified.

2. The 16,000 validation points are from TEN STATES, not "CONUS-wide," and ~5,253 (33%) are in Iowa alone. They are spatially clustered, so effective n is far below 16,000.

3. Validation points were deliberately restricted to fallow croplands "where the tile drainage signature is easily detectable"; the authors name unavailability of ground truth over vegetated cropland as the primary limitation. The accuracy figures are therefore optimistic.

4. Soils input is gSSURGO (10 m), not SSURGO. Iowa-specific accuracy is 91.1% (n=5,253), which strengthens the claim for this project's region. Do NOT cite the Table 1 Iowa area agreement of -0.04% as validation: the model iteratively relaxes its slope threshold until accumulated area meets the county census target, so county totals match by construction.

5. Add a redundancy caveat the claim omits: AgTile-US is a deterministic reallocation of county census totals + gSSURGO drainage class + SRTM slope, with step discontinuities at county boundaries. Given lat/lon are already the #2/#3 features, test it against a control arm that aggregates gSSURGO drainage class and slope directly, and report fold-level CIs — at 19 LOFO folds, PR-AUC deltas under ~0.03-0.05 are not distinguishable from noise. Also note the paper's own statement that tile drainage "greatly expanded since the late 1990s," so a 2017 snapshot over a 2008-2026 record is reliable for between-site RANK but not for absolute drained area in any given year. The GEE community-dataset mirror could not be verified and should be dropped or marked unconfirmed.

Claim is accurate in every checkable detail; two refinements. (1) METRIC: "86.03% accuracy" is NOT balanced/confusion-matrix accuracy — it is one-sided positive-class recall. The paper states "overall accuracy of 86.03% for the CONUS with an omission error of 13.97%" (sums to exactly 100%), because all 16,000 ground-truth points are known-DRAINED locations, manually identified from tile signatures visible on fallow cropland in ESRI 15m/1m/0.6m/0.3m imagery. No false-positive/commission rate is established anywhere in the paper; its limitations section concedes "uncertainty in croplands without tile drainage." So the layer's over-prediction rate is unquantified. (2) IOWA IS BETTER THAN CLAIMED: the claim quotes only the generic 82.7-93.6% Midwest band, but the paper reports Iowa specifically as the most tile-drained state (5.7 Mha) with 5,253 ground-truth points and 91.1% accuracy, and county-total bias of only +/-0.04% (Illinois +0.07%). Accuracy exceeds 98% on very-poorly/poorly-drained soils with slope <=1% — i.e. Des Moines Lobe conditions. Also note the paper's own Data Availability cites figshare DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.12668234, but that item contains only a metadata record (data.json, 275-byte CSV); the claim's URL (figshare 11825742) is the correct data item and is the one to use. Finally, the layer is not orthogonal information: within-county allocation is driven ONLY by gSSURGO drainage class + slope under a county census total, so basin-mean tile fraction is a smooth deterministic function of soil+slope+cropland. It is genuinely new relative to this project's current 68 features (which contain no soil drainage class, no slope, no county tile totals), but it should be expected to correlate with, not add to, any future soils feature.

The NWM is 1-km land-surface resolution routed to 2.7 million NHDPlus reaches. Modeled-Q error is therefore likely correlated WITH tile density, i.e. correlated with the very between-site gradient the model is trying to learn, so it can bias rather than merely add noise. corrections:
The claim is correct in substance and its central quote is exact. Four corrections, one of them materially changing the recommendation:

1. MAGNITUDE IS OVERSTATED -- the claim omits the calibration nuance, which is in the same abstract. Verbatim: "Employing a TD scheme enhanced the uncalibrated NWM performance by about 20-50% of the fully calibrated NWM (Calib)." That is, adding TD to the UNCALIBRATED model recovers only 20-50% of what calibration alone already achieves. The NWM retrospective is the CALIBRATED configuration, so calibration absorbs a large share of the missing-TD signal and the residual bias is smaller than "structurally mis-specified" implies. The direction of the claim survives, because CalibTD still beat Calib (higher event hit rates, lower false alarm rates, better high-flow estimation) -- so a residual deficit remains even after calibration. And crucially for this project, NWM calibration is performed at gauged basins and regionalized to ungauged reaches, so the compensation is weakest at exactly the arbitrary ungauged map pins the product targets. Net: caution justified, magnitude should be stated as "residual after calibration," not "raw structural omission."

2. "as of v2.0" IS NOT ESTABLISHED BY THIS SOURCE. The abstract says "the current NWM" with no version. Full text is unreachable (402/403 everywhere). Restate as "as of the paper's 2022 writing." The stronger and verifiable form: no NWM configuration through WRF-Hydro v5.4.0 (March 2025), which ships NWM v2.0/v2.1/v3.0 parameter tables, contains any tile-drainage scheme -- verified by source inspection, no OPT_TDRN, only generic QDRAIN bottom drainage. So v3.0 has NOT added TD, and the claim's open question is now closed in the claim's favor.

3. THE "ERROR CORRELATED WITH TILE DENSITY, SO IT BIASES RATHER THAN ADDS NOISE" STEP IS THE CLAIMANT'S INFERENCE, NOT THE PAPER'S FINDING. The paper reports no analysis of NWM error versus tile-drained fraction. The inference is plausible and directionally supported by the signs and magnitudes reported (peaks +14%, baseflow +11%, recharge -43 to -50%, all scaling with tile-drained fraction), but it must be labeled as inference, not as a published result. Practical implication: if NWM Q is used as a feature, include tile-drained fraction ALONGSIDE it so the model can learn and absorb the bias rather than inherit it.

4. Minor: the abstract says "2.7 million reaches," not "2.7 million NHDPlus reaches." NWM does route on NHDPlus v2.1, so the gloss is correct, but it is an addition to the source.

SEPARATE HIGH-VALUE FINDING -- THE PROJECT BRIEF CONTAINS A FACTUAL ERROR. The brief states tile drainage density is "NOT in the feature set, and NO data source has been identified yet." A data source exists, published by the SAME first author two years earlier, and it is free, CONUS-wide, and static -- i.e. precisely the between-site, static-geography kind of feature that is the only category that has ever worked on this project, encoding the control the brief itself calls dominant in Iowa:

AgTile-US. Valayamkunnath, Barlage, Chen, Gochis, Franz (2020), "Mapping of 30-meter resolution tile-drained croplands using a geospatial modeling approach," Scientific Data 7:257, DOI 10.1038/s41597-020-00596-x (open access, verified via Europe PMC PMC7406500).
- Resolution 30 m; binary raster (0 = undrained agricultural land, 1 = tile-drained).
- Coverage: entire CONUS, 65 deg 20' 46.49" W to 127 deg 53' 13.65" W, 22 deg 51' 41.18" N to 51 deg 36' 16.74" N. This covers ALL of Iowa AND the multi-state portions of the large basins -- it does not have the Iowa-boundary truncation problem that corrupts the current CDL/N-surplus inner join.
- Temporal: static, derived from USDA NASS 2017 Census of Agriculture county tile-drainage estimates, constrained by SSURGO soil drainage class and topographic slope via a per-county-calibrated decision tree. No time dimension, so it cannot go stale mid-record the way the 2017-terminating N-surplus does.
- Accuracy: validated against 16,000 ground-truth points, 86.03% CONUS-wide; 82.7-93.6% across the heavily tile-drained Midwest.
- Access: figshare, DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.11825742, landing page https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/AgTile-US/11825742 (record verified live via figshare API v2; title "AgTile-US", type dataset, posted 2020-07-13). GeoTIFF and NetCDF. Unrestricted public repository, no authentication, bulk download.
- License: CC BY 4.0; article is a US government work not under US copyright.
- Alternative/cross-check source noted in the same paper: Nakagaki et al. (USGS), 30-m gridded tile-drainage FRACTION (continuous, not binary) for the CONUS, updated with the 2012 USDA-NASS census for 12 Midwestern states.

Fit to this project: aggregate tile-drained fraction over basin cells in the existing 3 distance buckets, exactly like the CDL classes, giving 3 new static features. This is a static between-site variable, which is the only feature family that has produced gains here (geometry and static geography), and it targets the between_r2 0.21 / between_rate_r2 0.24 deficit that the brief identifies as holding essentially all remaining headroom. It requires no local nitrate history and no gauged neighbor, so it is fully compatible with the arbitrary-ungauged-map-pin deployment target. The n=19-independent-families constraint still applies and caps how much a handful of new static predictors can be expected to deliver -- 3 extra static columns fit against ~19 effective units risks overfitting the between-site term, so evaluate under LOFO and consider collapsing to a single basin-mean tile fraction before adding all three buckets.

The claim's factual core is exact and verified; three details need fixing, one of which weakens its key inference.

(1) n IS recoverable and the paper IS readable. 49 calibration basins (subset of the 1,469 NWM v2.0 CONUS calibration basins with TD >= 10% of area), regionalized to 939 HUC10 basins over the Upper Mississippi + Ohio HUC2s. Full text: Wayback copy of the NOAA PDF (web.archive.org/web/20250621042536id_/https://repository.library.noaa.gov/view/noaa/54925/noaa_54925_DS1.pdf). Wiley 402 and NOAA 403 are both bypassable.

(2) Split protocol must be recorded as TEMPORAL, NOT SPATIAL. Calibration 2007-10 to 2013-10, validation 2013-10 to 2019-10, same 49 basins. The Gower's-distance regionalization to 939 HUC10s is never scored against held-out gauges. So the "20-50%" figure is an out-of-time, in-sample-basin gain and is not an ungauged-basin result. Do not present it as evidence about transfer.

(3) THE INFERENCE OVERREACHES ON BIAS. The claim argues NWM-Q error "is likely correlated WITH tile density... so it can bias rather than merely add noise," implying a between-site LEVEL offset — the exact axis where our model has headroom. The paper's own numbers point the other way: "There are no considerable differences in the estimated Bias between Default and DefaultTD," and adding TD changes volume by only +2.3% while changing peaks +14% and baseflow +11%, with gains concentrated in NSE/KGE/COR/RMSE. The signature of the missing TD process is therefore predominantly TIMING, PEAK SHAPE and FLASHINESS — a within-site temporal distortion, which is the axis where our model already performs adequately (within_r2 0.42) — not a systematic between-site mean-flow bias. Additionally, the operational NWM is calibrated, and the CalibTD-noTile ablation shows calibration partially compensates for the missing physics; that compensation holds at gauged calibration basins and degrades at ungauged reaches only as far as donor-basin matching degrades. Net: the "structurally mis-specified" verdict is correct, but the specific escalation to "biases the between-site gradient" is unsupported by this source and should be downgraded to an untested hypothesis. Practical implication: NWM retrospective Q is still worth testing as a feature, but expect it to help WITHIN-site timing (already our strength) rather than fix between-site level, so its expected marginal value against our actual deficit is LOW.

(4) Minor: 2.7 million reaches is the v2.0 figure; SCN 23-76 states v3.0 covers "over 3.2 million river reaches." Use 2.7M only when describing the paper.

HIGH-VALUE COLLATERAL FIND — this paper directly closes the project's open "no tile-drainage data source identified" gap. It uses AgTile-US: a 30-m binary tile-drained-cropland map covering the CONUS (so it covers all of Iowa AND the out-of-state portions of the multi-state basins, unlike the Iowa-clipped CDL/N-surplus layers that currently under-count). Download: https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/AgTile-US/11825742 (figshare, free bulk download, no authentication; figshare datasets are CC-licensed — confirm the CC-BY/CC0 tag on the record page before redistribution). Static in time (a single snapshot, no year dimension — so no repeat of the "N-surplus broadcast forward" failure mode, since it is never presented as time-varying). It is a STATIC, GEOMETRIC, BETWEEN-SITE covariate — the exact class of feature that produced this project's only wins (lat, lon, log_basin_area) while every temporal feature failed. n=19-families caution: add it as ONE basin-mean tile fraction first, not as 3 distance-bucket copies; 3 new columns against 19 effective independent units is a real overfitting risk and the bucketed version should only be tried if the single-scalar version wins under LOFO.

The claim is substantially and quotably correct — the verbatim abstract sentence is exact, the NWM v2.0 attribution is confirmed in the methods, and the 1-km / 2.7-million-reach description is accurate. Four corrections:

(a) n IS recoverable and the paper is NOT effectively paywalled. It is a US Government work in the public domain; full text is retrievable through a text-extraction proxy on the NOAA repository PDF. Counts: 188 USGS gauges screened, 49 calibration basins (TD >= 10%), 139 gauges for regional evaluation over UMRB + ORB, WY2013-2019, plus South Fork Iowa River watershed for ET/soil-moisture validation.

(c) "Structurally mis-specified estimate of Q" overstates the residual bias in the retrospective products. It reports NO C-Q slope, NO chemostatic/dilution regime classification, NO between-site regression of concentration on N-input-yield / specific-discharge, and NO R2 for any nitrate prediction. THIS SOURCE THEREFORE DOES NOT ANSWER THE ASSIGNED RESEARCH QUESTION about C-Q behavior or about whether modeled discharge converts into between-site concentration skill; it answers a different question (the missing tile-drainage covariate). tier3_unverified.claim: Implementing a Hooghoudt tile-drainage scheme into NWM v2.0 over the heavily tile-drained upper Midwestern US produced these verbatim effects: 'Employing a TD scheme enhanced the uncalibrated NWM performance by about 20-50% of the fully calibrated NWM (Calib)'; 'The calibrated NWM with tile drainage (CalibTD) showed enhanced accuracy with higher event hit rates and lower false alarm rates than Calib'; 'CalibTD showed better performance in high-flow estimations as TD increased streamflow peaks (14%), volume (2.3%), and baseflow (11%).' Secondary sources report improvements in COR, NSE, NSE-with-weighting, and KGE significant at p<0.05 in all seasons for CalibTD vs Calib, and significant in winter and spring for the uncalibrated DefaultTD vs Default. FALSIFIABLE READ FOR THIS PROJECT: the sign and size of the tile effect on flow is 'peaks +14%, baseflow +11%, total volume only +2.3%' - i.e. tile drainage mainly RESHAPES the hydrograph rather than changing annual water yield. If nitrate concentration in Iowa is closer to chemostatic (C roughly flat in Q), then a +2.3% volume change implies tile density buys almost nothing through a dilution/specific-discharge channel, and its predictive value must instead come from flow-path partitioning (below).
tier3_unverified.effectSize: uncalibrated NWM+TD recovers 20-50% of full-calibration gain; peaks +14%, volume +2.3%, baseflow +11%; COR/NSE/KGE improvements p<0.05

NO leave-one-basin-out or spatial-transfer number is reported. This paper therefore provides NO evidence that NWM-derived Q is skillful at an ungauged arbitrary map pin, which is the deployment target.

tier3_unverified.claim: Regional water-balance effect of tile drainage in the NWM, verbatim: 'TD significantly reduced surface runoff (-7% to -29%), groundwater recharge (-43% to -50%), evapotranspiration (-7% to -13%), and soil moisture content (-2% to -3%). However, TD significantly increased soil profile lateral flow (27.7%) along with infiltration and soil water storage potential.' THIS IS THE MECHANISTIC ARGUMENT FOR TILE DENSITY AS A BETWEEN-SITE STATIC FEATURE: tile drainage converts a basin from a surface-runoff/recharge regime into a shallow-subsurface lateral-flow regime, and shallow subsurface lateral flow through the root zone is the dominant nitrate delivery pathway in Iowa. A -43% to -50% cut in groundwater recharge plus a +27.7% increase in lateral flow means two basins with IDENTICAL rainfall, identical crop mix and identical N surplus will deliver very different nitrate loads depending on tile density. That is precisely a between-site (level) effect, not a within-site (timing) effect - which matches this project's diagnosis that headroom is in the between-site term (between_r2 0.21 vs within_r2 0.42) and that seven temporal-feature ablations have failed.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: surface runoff -7% to -29%; groundwater recharge -43% to -50%; ET -7% to -13%; soil moisture -2% to -3%; soil-profile lateral flow +27.7%

tier3_unverified.nBasins: unknown - regional water-budget aggregation over the upper Midwest tile-drained domain (>10^5 km2), individual basin count not recoverable

What it DOES supply is a strong caution: the paper's whole premise is that the operational NWM misrepresents hydrology in tile-drained Midwest basins, and the residual it fixes is large (recovering 20-50% of what full calibration achieves). Judged against the deployment target, this argues for a specific ORDERING: take the free static AgTile-US tile fraction FIRST (cheap, static, no gauge required, works at any arbitrary map pin, directly targets the between-site deficit), and treat NWM-retrospective Q as a SEPARATE, LATER, and RISKIER experiment that must be validated against the project's own 22 USGS-gauged sites before it is trusted at the 63 ungauged ones - because at those 63 sites there is no way to detect NWM bias locally. Note also that the paper's own improvements come from CALIBRATING to gauges; the deployment target has no gauge, so the calibrated-configuration results do not transfer to it.

tier3_unverified.claim: Basu et al. (2010) explicitly report that nutrient (TN and TP) C-Q behavior in managed catchments is NON-chemostatic at the daily and monthly timescales, and that chemostasis emerges only after aggregation to the ANNUAL timescale: 'non-chemostatic responses are typical of nutrient (TN and TP) export from managed catchments in the MARB and BSDB (Figures S1 and S2). Notwithstanding non-chemostatic response at the daily or monthly time scales, we find consistent linear relationships (R2=0.7±0.2) between annual exported nutrient loads, LT, and annual discharge, QT.' This directly falsifies the naive inference that chemostasis licenses predicting DAILY nitrate concentration as a near-constant times discharge. For a project whose target is daily-max nitrate and a daily >=10 mg/L exceedance flag, the chemostatic result provides NO support at the operative timescale; the R2=0.7±0.2 applies to annual load vs annual discharge only.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: R2 = 0.7 +/- 0.2 for annual load vs annual discharge; daily/monthly explicitly non-chemostatic
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 21 MARB catchments (10^4-10^6 km2) + 14 Baltic Sea Drainage Basin catchments (10^2-10^5 km2), 10-30 years of record each

tier3_unverified.claim: Fitting the power-law C=AQ^b to DAILY water-quality monitoring data from the 21 MARB catchments, Basu et al. (2010) obtain a mean exponent mu_b = -0.02 with standard deviation sigma_b = 0.25 across all constituents. Split by type: geogenic (Type I) mu_b = -0.1, sigma_b = 0.2; anthropogenic (Type II, includes nitrate) mu_b = -0.09, sigma_b = 0.3; the two distributions differ significantly (Kruskal-Wallis p = 4.36e-13). The falsifiable operational consequence: with b near zero and sigma_b = 0.3, discharge explains very little DAILY concentration variance for nitrate-like constituents, and the site-to-site spread in b (sigma_b = 0.3) is as large as the mean signal — so a single global C-Q slope cannot be transferred to an unseen basin.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: mu_b = -0.02, sigma_b = 0.25 (all); Type I mu_b = -0.1, sigma_b = 0.2; Type II mu_b = -0.09, sigma_b = 0.3; Kruskal-Wallis p = 4.36e-13
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 21 MARB catchments for the b-value distribution; supplementary compilation adds 31 forested US/Puerto Rico catchments (10^1-10^3 km2), 3 Lake Okeechobee FL, 2 Swan River Basin (W. Australia)

tier3_unverified.claim: Basu et al. (2010) show the linear load-discharge relation is NOT diagnostic of chemostasis: they state that 'linear fits to the LT-QT relationship are judged adequate (R2>0.8) for a range of b values (-0.4<b<1.4)', a criterion 'satisfied for all observed b values for Type II constituents and 90% of the b values for Type I constituents.' They further acknowledge the prior critique that the L-Q correlation 'is a spurious correlation since discharge is a component of load calculation.' Falsifiable implication for this project: switching the modeling target from concentration to LOAD (C x Q) would manufacture an R2>0.8 that is largely an artifact of Q appearing on both sides, and back-deriving concentration as L/Q would recover none of the between-site concentration skill — the apparent gain would be spurious by the paper's own admission.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: linear L-Q fits give R2>0.8 across the whole range -0.4<b<1.4, i.e. R2>0.8 is attained even for strongly non-chemostatic C-Q behavior
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 21 MARB + 14 BSDB

tier3_unverified.claim: The central quantity Basu et al. (2010) propose for between-site prediction is the annual flow-weighted concentration Cf_bar = LT/QT, which they show is temporally invariant per catchment and which they call 'a constant, mean annual, flow-weighted concentration ... as a useful index for effective biogeochemical stationarity.' Crucially, the paper treats Cf_bar as an EMPIRICALLY FITTED per-catchment constant (the slope of the linear LT-QT fit), and provides NO model, regression, or R2 predicting Cf_bar from N inputs, N surplus, land use, or specific discharge across sites. The paper therefore does not supply the between-site relation this project needs; it only asserts that 'the anthropogenic drivers (e.g., land-use; nutrient inputs) are reflected in Cf_bar' without quantifying that link. Anyone citing Basu 2010 as evidence that concentration ~ N-input-yield / specific-discharge is a validated between-site predictor is over-reading it.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: no reported R2 for any between-site model of Cf_bar; Cf_bar is a per-site fitted slope requiring that site's own paired C and Q observations
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 21 MARB + 14 BSDB (Cf_bar fitted separately per catchment, not predicted from covariates)

tier3_unverified.claim: Basu et al. (2010) report that annual flow-weighted nitrate/TN concentration in the MARB stayed temporally invariant DESPITE an approximately 1.5-fold increase in nutrient inputs over the preceding three decades, and that in the Baltic Sea Drainage Basin 'concerted efforts to decrease nutrient inputs towards a target level of ~50% have failed to show positive results.' They cite MARB nitrate trend data showing 'stable concentrations after 1975, in contrast to increasing trends in the previous 25 years (1950-1975).' The falsifiable prediction for this project: contemporary N-input covariates should have WEAK explanatory power for a catchment's mean nitrate level in a legacy-dominated system, because export is 'transport- rather than supply-limited, such that contemporary distributed and point sources have lesser influence.' This is consistent with, and offers a mechanistic explanation for, this project's observed failure of the 2017 gTREND nitrogen-surplus feature (broadcasting surplus forward scored -0.166) — contemporary surplus is the wrong state variable; accumulated legacy soil/groundwater N storage is.

tier3_unverified.nBasins: 21 MARB + 14 BSDB

tier3_unverified.claim: Basu et al. (2010) bound the domain where the discharge-surrogate approach works, and the failures are informative: in the Hubbard Brook (US) catchment, 'under conditions of minimal anthropogenic influence, and resulting low nitrate concentrations, the LT-QT relationship lacked any significant correlation,' while at the SAME site the geogenic constituent sodium showed significant linear correlation. Pesticides likewise show supply-limited scatter because half-lives of '1 to 100 days ... preclude the buildup of legacy sources.' They also caution that 'under land-use change scenarios, the timescale over which the assumption of stationarity is valid is a function of the accumulated legacy stores and their rate of depletion.' Falsifiable consequence: the Q-as-surrogate strategy degrades precisely at the low-concentration, low-legacy end of the gradient — which for an Iowa violation classifier is the sub-10 mg/L population that dominates the 73.7% negative class, so discharge-derived features should be expected to help least exactly where the classifier's false-alarm problem lives.

(2024) predicted 7-day backward-looking average nitrate concentration at 46 predominantly agricultural sites in the midwestern and eastern US using LSTMs fed daily OBSERVED discharge plus meteorological variables and static watershed attributes (anthropogenic hydrologic modification, N application, climate, groundwater, land use/land cover, physiography, soils). Single-site models — one model trained AND tested at each individual location — achieved median Kling-Gupta Efficiency = 0.66. Because train and test come from the same site, this is a TEMPORAL holdout at a gauged site, NOT a spatial holdout, and it is therefore NOT comparable to our LOFO 0.820 AUC / R2 0.328. The paper's own framing is 'at intensively monitored sites'; no prediction-in-ungauged-basin nitrate skill number appears in the abstract or data-release description.

(2024) report that pooling all 46 sites into a single global LSTM 'reduced performance at several locations with distinct characteristics, suggesting that there is a threshold of dissimilarity beyond which more data does not improve the model,' and explicitly note that 'while many deep learning studies have shown that national or even global models can outperform local models, it is not clear that this is true for water quality constituents.' This falsifies the naive transfer of the CAMELS streamflow finding (that a single pooled model beats per-basin models) to nitrate, and predicts that adding more distant, dissimilar catchments to our 19 families may not buy between-site skill.

tier3_unverified.claim: Gorski et al. (2024) compared four pooling schemes across the same 46 sites: (a) 46 single-site models, (b) 5 cluster models with sites clustered by basin attributes, (c) 8 'hydro terrane' models grouping sites by glacial hydrogeologic terrane, and (d) 1 global model. Accuracy at poorly performing sites 'could be improved by grouping sites with similar characteristics.' This is a falsifiable, directly testable design for our project: group the 19 basin families by static attribute similarity (or by Iowa landform region / glacial terrane — Des Moines Lobe vs Iowan Surface vs Southern Iron Clay vs Loess Hills) and fit per-group models, rather than one pooled model or per-site models. Note the caveat: 5-8 groups over 46 sites is ~6-9 sites per group; at 19 families the equivalent gives ~2-4 families per group, which is likely below the point where a group-specific model can be fit at all.
