(2024) title claim and abstract finding: 'Across all sites, discharge and watershed soil and physiographic attributes showed a strong influence on model performance.' CRITICAL QUALIFICATION FOR OUR DEPLOYMENT TARGET: the discharge used was daily OBSERVED discharge at gauged, intensively monitored sites — not modeled discharge, and not available at an arbitrary map pin. The paper therefore supports the hypothesis that discharge carries first-order nitrate information, but provides ZERO evidence that a MODELED discharge surrogate (e.g. NWM v3 retrospective at the joined COMID) retains that information, and zero evidence that the discharge signal transfers to an unmonitored site. The co-equal finding — that watershed SOIL and PHYSIOGRAPHIC static attributes are also strongly influential — is the transferable half, and is exactly the between-site static information our feature set currently lacks (we have no soil, no drainage/tile, no physiographic attributes beyond lat/lon/area).

(2024) found 'considerable regional differences related to controlling processes such as groundwater contributions' in the cross-site driver analysis — i.e. the drivers of nitrate are not stationary across regions, and the same input carries different information in a groundwater-dominated catchment versus a surface/tile-dominated one. Falsifiable implication for our project: a single global XGBoost fit over all 19 Iowa basin families implicitly assumes driver stationarity that this paper reports is violated even within the agricultural Midwest; per-region (Des Moines Lobe vs driftless/loess) driver contrast is a testable prediction, and groundwater-contribution attributes (e.g. baseflow index, glacial terrane class) are candidate static features.

Secondary sources citing the paper add that nitrate in the UMRB is chemodynamic at low flows but chemostatic at high flows (fitted as a BROKEN power law with a fitted breakpoint, not a single power law), and that the chemostatic domain contributes a median = 71% of the annual NO3 load. tier3_unverified.claim: DIRECT NEGATIVE RESULT AGAINST THE RESEARCH HYPOTHESIS (discharge -> between-site skill). Recomputed from the paper's own dataset, n=32 UMRB sites with PERFECT, MEASURED, CO-LOCATED USGS discharge: mean specific discharge is nearly worthless as a between-site predictor of nitrate level. Univariate R2 of log10(mean specific discharge) against between-site responses: mean nitrate R2 = 0.034; log10 mean nitrate R2 = 0.027; fraction of days >= 10 mg/L R2 = 0.097. In multiple regression for between-site mean nitrate, adding log10(mean specific discharge) to a %row-crop + %tile model moves R2 from 0.486 to 0.487 (delta R2 = +0.001); further adding log10(area) leaves it at 0.487. By contrast %agriculture alone gives R2 = 0.539 and %forest alone R2 = 0.550 for the same response. CRITICAL IMPLICATION: since this null is obtained with real gauged discharge, a MODELED discharge source (NWM v3 retrospective, SPARROW mean-annual flow) can only perform worse once model error is added — modeled-Q error would be added on top of a signal that is already near zero at the between-site level. The C = N-yield / specific-discharge dilution-mass-balance framing is NOT supported as a between-site relation in this dataset. Discharge is a WITHIN-site timing variable, not a between-site level variable — which matches this project's own diagnosis ("a good timer, a mediocre site-ranker") and its seven failed temporal-feature ablations.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: log10(mean specific Q) alone: R2=0.034 (mean NO3), 0.097 (exceedance fraction). Added to crops+tile: R2 0.486 -> 0.487, delta = +0.001

tier3_unverified.claim: CLEAN SEPARATION BETWEEN 'WHAT CONTROLS DYNAMICS' AND 'WHAT CONTROLS LEVEL' — recomputed from the paper's dataset, n=32. The C-Q variability ratio CVc/CVq is a SCALE/NETWORK property and is essentially unrelated to land use: log10(CVc/CVq) vs log10(basin area) R2 = 0.412 (slope +0.127, i.e. concentration variability rises relative to discharge variability as basins get bigger, confirming the paper's headline), but vs % tile drainage R2 = 0.001, vs % row crop R2 = 0.034, vs % agriculture R2 = 0.095. Conversely the LEVEL of nitrate is a land-use property and NOT a scale property: mean nitrate vs log10(area) R2 = 0.119 while vs % agriculture R2 = 0.539. The fitted power-law intercept log10(a) (concentration at unit specific discharge, i.e. the site's absolute level after removing flow) is likewise land-use controlled: vs %agriculture R2 = 0.585, vs %forest R2 = 0.649, vs %row crop R2 = 0.513, vs %tile R2 = 0.251, but vs log10(area) only R2 = 0.179. ACTIONABLE READ FOR THIS PROJECT: the between-site deficit should be attacked with STATIC LAND-USE / TILE covariates, not with basin size, not with discharge, and not with more temporal features — which is consistent with the project's finding that only geometry and static geography have ever produced wins.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: log10(CVc/CVq): area R2=0.412 vs tile R2=0.001. Power-law intercept log10(a): %ag R2=0.585, %forest R2=0.649 vs area R2=0.179

tier3_unverified.claim: OPERATIONAL DATASET — this closes the project's stated gap that 'tile drainage density: known to be the dominant hydrologic control in Iowa, NOT in the feature set, and NO data source has been identified yet'. Marinos et al. (2020) source their tile layer from Nakagaki, N., and Wieczorek, M.E., 2016, 'Estimates of subsurface tile drainage extent for 12 Midwest states, 2012', U.S. Geological Survey data release (confirmed in the paper's archived Step3_Compile_LULC.R: 'This data was extracted from Nakagaki et al., cited in paper using QGIS and the basin shapefiles'). SPECIFICATION: 30 m raster; each cell stores estimated tile-drained area in SQUARE METRES, so the fraction of a cell that is tile-drained = value/900 (this is exactly the conversion in the paper's code: Tiled = Tiledmean/900). Static single-epoch product (2012 Census of Agriculture), no time dimension. Built from 2012 Census of Agriculture state-level tile acreage + NLCD 2011 cultivated cropland + STATSGO2 poorly/moderately drained soils. COVERAGE: 12 Midwest states — SD, NE, KS, MN, IA, MO, WI, IL, MI, IN, OH, KY — which covers ALL of Iowa AND the out-of-state portions of Iowa's multi-state basins (MN, SD, NE, MO, IL headwaters), i.e. it does NOT suffer the Iowa-only clipping problem that currently under-counts CDL crop area and N surplus. DOI 10.5066/F7W37TDP. Access: free public bulk download, no authentication, from https://www.sciencebase.gov/catalog/item/55f6e42ae4b0477df11bff10 (mirror: https://data.usgs.gov/datacatalog/data/USGS:55f6e42ae4b0477df11bff10). USGS data release — public domain / no license restriction. CAVEAT: the paper had to set tile = NA for its one Mississippi-mainstem site (07020850) because the basin extended beyond the 12-state layer, so any basin reaching outside the 12 states needs an explicit NaN/partial-coverage flag rather than a silent inner join. A newer alternative if higher fidelity is wanted: Valayamkunnath et al. 2020, 'Mapping of 30-meter resolution tile-drained croplands using a geospatial modeling approach', Scientific Data 7:257, DOI 10.1038/s41597-020-00596-x.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: 30 m raster, m2 tile-drained per 900 m2 cell; 12 Midwest states; single epoch 2012; DOI 10.5066/F7W37TDP
tier3_unverified.nBasins: not-applicable (gridded covariate, not a model)

tier3_unverified.claim: C-Q REGIME FOR NITRATE IN THIS REGION IS MOBILIZATION/ENRICHMENT, NOT DILUTION — and discharge explains less than half of within-site daily nitrate variance even where it is measured. Recomputed from the paper's dataset (OLS log10(C) ~ log10(specific Q) on daily values, n=32 sites): the C-Q exponent b is POSITIVE at 32 of 32 sites, range +0.090 to +1.095, median +0.440. Not a single site dilutes on the daily-mean timescale. The within-site coefficient of determination of that log-log C-Q fit ranges R2 = 0.026 to 0.869 with MEDIAN R2 = 0.417 — so at the median site, perfectly measured co-located discharge explains only ~42% of daily log-nitrate variance. The C-Q exponent b is itself weakly land-use controlled (vs %row crop R2 = 0.345, vs %agriculture R2 = 0.310, vs %tile R2 = 0.209, vs log10(area) R2 = 0.147), meaning b is not reliably transferable to an ungauged pin from static attributes either. IMPLICATION FOR TARGET DEFINITION: because b > 0 everywhere, LOAD (C x Q) scales roughly as Q^(1+b) with 1+b in the range 1.09-2.10, so a load target is even more dominated by discharge than a concentration target; back-deriving concentration from a modeled load would divide by a modeled Q and propagate NWM discharge error directly into the concentration estimate. Given that measured Q already fails as a between-site predictor (R2 = 0.034), switching the target to load is NOT supported by this dataset as a route to between-site skill. CAVEAT ON MY NUMBERS: the paper fits a broken power law by maximum likelihood on flow-weighted daily concentrations; I fit a single OLS log-log line on unweighted daily means, so my b values are comparable in sign and order but are not the paper's published estimates.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: C-Q exponent b positive at 32/32 sites, range +0.090 to +1.095, median +0.440; within-site log-log C-Q R2 median 0.417 (range 0.026-0.869)

tier3_unverified.claim: Basu et al. (2010) fitted daily water-quality monitoring data from the Mississippi-Atchafalaya River Basin (MARB) catchments to the C-Q power function C=AQ^b and found the exponent b had a mean of -0.02 with standard deviation 0.25, which they interpret as "an overall chemostatic response for these constituents." Splitting by constituent type, geogenic (Type I) constituents had mu_b = -0.1, sigma_b = 0.2 and anthropogenic (Type II, includes nitrate/TN and TP) had mu_b = -0.09, sigma_b = 0.3, with the two distributions statistically different (Kruskal-Wallis p = 4.36 x 10^-13). DIRECT CONSEQUENCE FOR THIS PROJECT: b near zero is the definition of chemostasis and means concentration is nearly INDEPENDENT of discharge at a given site. If Iowa agricultural nitrate is chemostatic in this sense, then adding a discharge feature (modeled NWM Q or otherwise) is predicted to add little or nothing to CONCENTRATION or threshold-exceedance prediction, even though it would strongly predict LOAD. This is the central falsifiable test of the research question, and this paper's own numbers argue AGAINST the discharge-as-savior hypothesis for a concentration target.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: C-Q power-law exponent b: all MARB constituents mu_b=-0.02, sigma_b=0.25; Type I geogenic mu_b=-0.1, sigma_b=0.2; Type II anthropogenic mu_b=-0.09, sigma_b=0.3; Kruskal-Wallis p=4.36e-13
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: not-applicable — descriptive in-sample power-law fits to observed C-Q pairs, no predictive train/test split of any kind
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 21 MARB catchments (10^4 to 10^6 km2) for the primary b-value distribution; supplemented by 31 forested catchments (10^1-10^3 km2) in continental US and Puerto Rico, 3 Lake Okeechobee (FL) catchments, and 2 Swan River Basin (W. Australia) catchments

tier3_unverified.claim: The paper's headline quantitative result is that ANNUAL exported nutrient load L_T is a linear function of ANNUAL discharge Q_T with "consistent linear relationships (R2=0.7±0.2) between annual exported nutrient loads, L_T, and annual discharge, Q_T" for total-N and total-P. CRITICAL SCOPE LIMITS that must be stated when citing this number: (a) it is an INTER-ANNUAL, WITHIN-CATCHMENT regression — each catchment gets its own fit and its own slope — NOT a between-catchment regression, so it is NOT evidence that discharge predicts the absolute level of an unseen basin; (b) the target is LOAD, not concentration, and load contains Q on both sides of the equation, a spurious-correlation problem the authors explicitly acknowledge ("it is a spurious correlation since discharge is a component of load calculation"); (c) the timescale is ANNUAL, roughly 10-30 annual points per catchment, not daily. It provides no support for daily-resolution concentration or exceedance prediction.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Annual load vs annual discharge linear fit R2 = 0.7 +/- 0.2 for TN and TP
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: not-applicable — in-sample ordinary least squares fits per catchment on annual aggregates; no held-out spatial, temporal, or random split
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 21 MARB catchments (10^4-10^6 km2) plus 14 Baltic Sea Drainage Basin catchments (10^2-10^5 km2); record length 10 to 30 years per catchment

tier3_unverified.claim: The paper reports that annual flow-weighted concentration (Cf = L_T/Q_T) is TEMPORALLY INVARIANT within a catchment "even with significant (~1.5 times) increase in nutrient inputs over the last three decades in the MARB," and that in the Baltic Sea Drainage Basin "concerted efforts to decrease nutrient inputs towards a target level of ~50% have failed to show positive results." Supporting trend evidence: nitrate concentrations in the MARB were stable after 1975 in contrast to increasing trends over the previous 25 years (1950-1975). FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION FOR THIS PROJECT'S FEATURES: contemporary annual nitrogen input/surplus is decoupled from stream nitrate concentration on decadal timescales, because legacy subsurface N stores buffer it. This independently explains the project's observed negative result that broadcasting 2017 N-surplus forward in time HURT performance (-0.166) — the temporal dimension of an N-surplus feature carries little signal even in principle. It also predicts, conversely, that a TIME-INVARIANT per-basin N-legacy or long-term-mean-surplus static feature is the better parameterization than a time-varying one.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Nutrient inputs rose ~1.5x over three decades in MARB with no corresponding change in annual flow-weighted concentration; BSDB ~50% input-reduction target produced no detected improvement; MARB nitrate concentrations stable post-1975 vs rising 1950-1975
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: not-applicable — long-term observational trend description, not a predictive model
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 21 MARB catchments plus 14 BSDB catchments (35 total)

tier3_unverified.claim: Basu et al. propose that each catchment "may be characterized with a constant, mean annual, flow-weighted concentration (slope of the linear fit in Figure 1), Cf, as a useful index for 'effective biogeochemical stationarity'," and state that "annual nutrient loads can be robustly estimated as L_T = Q_T * Cf, where the hydro-climatic controls (e.g., precipitation, evapotranspiration) are manifested in Q_T, and the anthropogenic drivers (e.g., land-use; nutrient inputs) are reflected in Cf." IMPORTANT NEGATIVE FINDING FOR THE RESEARCH QUESTION: although this framing implies exactly the between-site relation the project is looking for (a per-basin concentration constant set by land use and N inputs), THE PAPER NEVER FITS OR REPORTS IT. There is no regression of Cf on N input, N surplus, specific discharge, or any land-use covariate, and NO between-catchment R2 is reported anywhere in the paper. Cf is obtained empirically as a per-catchment fitted slope from that catchment's OWN observed loads — which requires local nitrate observations and therefore is NOT available at an arbitrary ungauged, unmonitored map pin. Cited as support for a predictive between-site C ~ input/discharge relation, this paper is a decomposition framework, not evidence.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Zero — no between-catchment regression of Cf on nutrient inputs or specific discharge is reported; no cross-site R2 appears in the paper
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: not-applicable — the between-site predictive relation implied by the framework was never estimated or validated
tier3_unverified.nBasins: n/a — the between-site analysis was not performed

tier3_unverified.claim: The paper's own counter-example establishes that chemostatic/linear L-Q behavior for nitrate is CONDITIONAL on accumulated anthropogenic legacy, not universal: "Our analysis of data from the Hubbard Brook (US) catchment showed that, under conditions of minimal anthropogenic influence, and resulting low nitrate concentrations, the L_T-Q_T relationship lacked any significant correlation. At the same site, however, the geogenic constituent sodium, exhibited significant linear correlation." Pesticides behave the same supply-limited way because short half-lives ("1 to 100 days") preclude legacy buildup. The authors conclude nutrient export from managed catchments is "transport- rather than supply-limited, such that contemporary distributed and point sources have lesser influence on inter-annual fluctuations in stream nutrient concentrations." IMPLICATION: the discharge-as-predictor logic applies only where legacy N is large. Iowa row-crop basins plausibly qualify, but the strength of any Q-based feature should be expected to VARY BETWEEN BASINS as a function of legacy N accumulation — meaning a single global discharge coefficient may underperform, and the between-site term the project needs is legacy-N magnitude, which discharge itself does not carry.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Hubbard Brook nitrate annual L-Q: no significant correlation (qualitative, no R2 given); sodium at the same site: significant linear correlation; pesticide half-lives 1-100 days cited as reason legacy cannot accumulate
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: not-applicable — descriptive correlation analysis on observed annual data
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 1 (Hubbard Brook) for the nitrate counter-example; 31 forested US/Puerto Rico catchments in the broader supplementary compilation

tier3_unverified.claim: SCALE AND RESOLUTION MISMATCH — the strongest caveat on transferring this paper to the Iowa virtual-sensor problem. The catchments analyzed are 10^4 to 10^6 km2 (MARB, i.e. whole-Mississippi-scale) and 10^2 to 10^5 km2 (Baltic), and every headline result is at the ANNUAL aggregation scale. The paper states plainly that at finer resolution the opposite behavior holds: "non-chemostatic responses are typical of nutrient (TN and TP) export from managed catchments in the MARB and BSDB" at the DAILY or MONTHLY time scales. The linear-L-Q criterion is also loose: linear fits are "judged adequate (R2>0.8) for a range of b values (-0.4<b<1.4)," a band wide enough to include strong dilution AND strong mobilization, so an R2>0.8 annual load fit does NOT establish that concentration is flat. Since this project predicts DAILY-MAX concentration and daily threshold exceedance on basins far smaller than 10^4 km2, the paper's chemostatic conclusion is outside its demonstrated domain, and its daily-scale statement actively predicts that daily nitrate is NOT chemostatic — which is the regime where a discharge feature could still help.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Catchment areas 10^4-10^6 km2 (MARB) and 10^2-10^5 km2 (BSDB); chemostasis claimed only at annual scale; explicit statement of non-chemostatic daily/monthly nutrient response; linear L-Q judged adequate (R2>0.8) across b in (-0.4, 1.4)
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: not-applicable — no predictive validation performed at any timescale
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 21 MARB + 14 BSDB = 35 catchments in the primary analysis

tier3_unverified.claim: OPERATIONAL TILE-DRAINAGE DATA SOURCE EXISTS AND IS PUBLIC — DIRECTLY FILLS THE PROJECT'S KNOWN #1 DATA GAP. Gorski & Zimmer (2021, HESS 25:1333, doi:10.5194/hess-25-1333-2021) state in Sect. 2.2: 'Data for landforms, drainage infrastructure, and stream network were downloaded from the Iowa Department of Natural Resources.' They compute 'drainage infrastructure density' in units of km of built drainage per km^2 of watershed (a line-density of mapped tile drains, ditches, and canals), reporting 1.11 km km^-2 for the heavily drained Upstream Sac City watershed and 0.37 km km^-2 for the least-drained Middle Redfield watershed. Figure 1 maps 'built drainage infrastructure' as gray line features across the entire 8,870 km^2 Raccoon River basin. FALSIFIABLE: a mapped built-drainage line layer for Iowa is obtainable free from the Iowa DNR NRGIS library (https://www.iowadnr.gov/ , NRGIS geodata portal), and basin-level line-density (km/km^2) can be computed per delineated basin. CAVEATS THE PAPER FORCES: (a) the paper gives no URL, no layer name, no vintage, and no statement of statewide completeness — the layer must be independently verified before any claim of Iowa-wide coverage; (b) it is explicitly an IOWA agency product, so it will NOT cover the multi-state portions of the project's largest basins, exactly reproducing the existing crop/N-surplus under-counting bias for out-of-state area; (c) it is a static attribute with no time dimension, which is what the project wants — every temporal feature has failed, and this is a purely between-site static geographic variable of the type that has been the project's only source of wins.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Drainage infrastructure density ranged 0.37 to 1.11 km km^-2 across the 5 study watersheds; units km per km^2
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 5 nested watersheds (Raccoon River, central Iowa); layer coverage is statewide Iowa but unverified in this paper

tier3_unverified.claim: TILE-DRAINAGE DENSITY EXPLAINS BETWEEN-SITE DIFFERENCES IN ANNUAL NITRATE LOAD AT R^2 = 0.71-0.88 — THE EXACT BETWEEN-SITE TERM THIS PROJECT IS MISSING. Gorski & Zimmer (2021) Fig. 7 regresses cumulative annual NO3 load (kg N km^-2 yr^-1) against drainage infrastructure density across their five watersheds and report 'Stormflow – R^2 = 0.71' and 'Baseflow – R^2 = 0.75'. Restricted to spring (April-June), 'both baseflow and stormflow NO3 loads are strongly correlated with drainage infrastructure density (R^2 = 0.88 and 0.88, respectively; p < 0.05)'. Concentrations order the same way: median NO3 was 9.23 +/- 3.09 mg L^-1 at the most heavily tile-drained site (USC, 1.11 km km^-2) versus 6.96 +/- 2.51 mg L^-1 at the least-drained site (MRF, 0.37 km km^-2), with the basin outlet DVM intermediate at 7.38 +/- 3.07 mg L^-1. Text: 'There is a systematic trend toward higher-NO3 load in watersheds with a higher density of built drainage infrastructure.' FALSIFIABLE PREDICTION FOR THIS PROJECT: adding basin-mean drainage-infrastructure density as a static feature should raise between_r2 / between_rate_r2 (currently 0.21 / 0.24) more than any temporal feature tried so far, because the ~2.3 mg L^-1 spread in median concentration it explains is a between-SITE level offset, not a within-site timing signal. HARD CAVEAT ON SAMPLE SIZE: every R^2 quoted here is fitted to FIVE points (3 degrees of freedom), IN-SAMPLE, with no held-out validation of any kind; an R^2 of 0.88 on n=5 is not distinguishable from noise at conventional power. Worse, the five watersheds are NESTED (MJF contains USC; MRF contains UPN; DVM contains all), so the effective independent sample is smaller than 5 — this is the same nesting problem that collapses this project's 85 sites to 19 families. Treat these R^2 values as a hypothesis-generating direction, NOT as an expected effect size.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Annual load vs drainage density: R^2 = 0.71 (stormflow), 0.75 (baseflow); spring-only R^2 = 0.88 and 0.88, p < 0.05. Median NO3 spread 6.96 to 9.23 mg L^-1 across the drainage-density gradient. Annual export ranged 4216 +/- 768 kg N km^-2 yr^-1 (USC) to 2222 +/- 371 kg N km^-2 yr^-1 (MRF)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 5 (nested, so effective n < 5)

tier3_unverified.claim: STORMFLOW NITRATE IS CHEMOSTATIC — THIS IS A DIRECT ARGUMENT THAT MODELED DISCHARGE WILL NOT BUY CONCENTRATION SKILL IN THE HIGH-CONCENTRATION REGIME THAT DRIVES VIOLATIONS. Gorski & Zimmer (2021) partitioned 4 years of daily data (2016-2019) into stormflow and baseflow and fitted log-log c-Q slopes (chemostatic defined as |slope| <= 0.2, enrichment > 0.2, dilution < -0.2). They report: 'Stormflow showed consistent chemostatic patterns across all seasons' and, for individually fitted storm events, 'event-averaged c-Q slopes form a narrow distribution around zero across all seasons' (Fig. 5a histogram, ~15 events per watershed per year x 5 watersheds x 4 years). Also: 'Although tile-drained watersheds show higher stormflow NO3 concentrations (Fig. 3b), there does not appear to be a systematic effect on stormflow c-Q slopes (Fig. 4b). This indicates that the nitrate sources activated during stormflow are transport limited across all watersheds.' Mechanistically: 'landscapes with such agricultural intensity are a saturated solute source for which delivery is flow limited' (citing Thompson et al., 2011). IMPLICATION AGAINST THE RESEARCH ANGLE: a c-Q slope of ~0 means concentration is approximately INVARIANT to discharge during storms. Knowing Q at an ungauged site — however obtained, NWM retrospective or otherwise — therefore carries near-zero marginal information about C during exactly the periods when maximum daily nitrate (and hence the >= 10 mg L^-1 violation flag) is highest. This predicts that a modeled-Q feature will fail the same way the seven prior hydrologic temporal features failed. The information that DOES separate sites is the chemostatic PLATEAU LEVEL (the intercept a in C = aQ^b), which this paper attributes to static landscape attributes — drainage density and cropped area — not to Q.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Stormflow event-averaged c-Q slopes distributed narrowly around 0 across all seasons and all 5 watersheds; spring export regimes chemostatic with average c-Q slope 0.15 (stormflow) and 0.18 (baseflow); ~15 storm events per watershed per year over 4 years

tier3_unverified.claim: BASEFLOW C-Q IS SEASONALLY NON-STATIONARY AND ITS SLOPE IS NEGATIVELY CORRELATED WITH TILE DRAINAGE (SPRING R^2 = 0.85) — MEANING ANY SINGLE C-Q PARAMETER PER SITE IS THE WRONG ABSTRACTION. Gorski & Zimmer (2021): all five watersheds showed enriching baseflow behavior annually, with slopes from 0.21 (USC, most tile-drained) to 0.79 (UPN, least drained). Seasonally, summer baseflow was strongly chemodynamic (average c-Q slope 0.73 across all watersheds; DVM summer = 0.75) while spring baseflow was chemostatic (DVM spring = 0.08). The tile-drainage control: 'There is a negative correlation between seasonal baseflow c-Q slope and drainage infrastructure density, which is strongest during the spring months (R^2 = 0.85; p < 0.05).' Mechanism: heavy built drainage 'serves to homogenize baseflow sources', eliminating the low-flow / low-NO3 periods that create enrichment slopes; the end-members are MRF (0.37 km km^-2) which was chemodynamic in every season (0.34 winter to 0.75 summer) versus USC (1.11 km km^-2) which was chemostatic in every season except summer (0.29). CONSEQUENCE FOR FEATURE DESIGN: the sign and magnitude of any Q-to-C relationship flips by season AND by tile-drainage density, so a global Q feature is mis-specified; if Q is used at all it must be interacted with season and with drainage density. Note this also predicts a QUALITATIVE interaction the project could test cheaply with its existing 22 gauged sites before ever touching NWM. n=5 caveat applies to the R^2 = 0.85 (five nested points, in-sample, no held-out validation).
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Baseflow c-Q slope vs drainage density: R^2 = 0.85, p < 0.05 (spring). Annual baseflow slopes 0.21-0.79. Summer baseflow slope average 0.73; spring baseflow chemostatic (DVM 0.08 vs 0.75 summer)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 5 (nested)

tier3_unverified.claim: EXPLICIT NEGATIVE RESULT: C-Q SLOPES ARE UNSTABLE TO A HANDFUL OF DAYS AND DO NOT CORRELATE WITH WATERSHED AREA — THE AUTHORS WARN AGAINST SINGLE-PARAMETER C-Q CHARACTERIZATION. Gorski & Zimmer (2021) Sect. 3.5 document that in UPN, two anomalous low-flow low-NO3 events in October 2017 (mean 1.34 and 0.46 mg L^-1) shifted the fall bulk stormflow c-Q slope from 0.09 to 0.71 despite representing '<1 % of annual flow and NO3 load'. In MJF, an anomalous low-flow period (mean 96 cfs, <0.1 flow percentile) from 26 July to 19 October 2017 changed the annual baseflow c-Q slope from 0.42 to 1.42 — a factor of 3.4 from one ~3-month low-flow window. The authors conclude: 'The ability of a single anomalous period (whether real or due to sensor artifacts) to influence the overall characterization of a hydrologic system highlights the difficulty in representing nutrient export behavior based on a single parameter fit across several seasons and flow regimes.' Separately: 'Seasonal and annual c-Q slopes across all hydrologic regimes show only weak correlations with watershed area' — i.e. the one static attribute the project ALREADY has (log_basin_area) does not predict c-Q behavior. They also state their records 'do not cover a sufficient length of time to thoroughly examine interannual variability, and it remains an open question as to how stable the c-Q patterns presented in this study are over time.' FALSIFIABLE PREDICTION: fitting a per-site c-Q slope as an engineered feature on this project's 22 gauged sites will produce estimates whose leave-one-out variance exceeds their between-site spread, and it will not transfer to the 63 ungauged sites at all — c-Q slope is not derivable without Q AND C at the target, which the deployment target has neither of.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Single anomalous period changed annual baseflow c-Q slope from 0.42 to 1.42 (3.4x); two events comprising <1% of annual flow changed seasonal stormflow slope from 0.09 to 0.71 (7.9x). c-Q slope vs watershed area: 'only weak correlations' (no R^2 given)

tier3_unverified.claim: RIPARIAN CROPPED AREA WITHIN 100 m OF THE STREAM EXPLAINS SUMMER BASEFLOW NITRATE LOAD AT R^2 = 0.94 — A MUCH TIGHTER BUFFER THAN THE 0-2 km RIPARIAN BUCKET THIS PROJECT ALREADY TESTED. Gorski & Zimmer (2021): 'The baseflow NO3 load during the summer is most strongly correlated with the percentage of cropped area within 100 m of the stream (R^2 = 0.94; p < 0.01)', concluding 'land use near the stream has a large impact on NO3 loadings, indicating that buffer strips or other near-stream management practices may be effective management practices for reducing loads during these periods' and 'land use in riparian areas exhibits strong influence on baseflow nitrate loads'. Land use was NLCD 2016 at 30 m x 30 m (Dewitz, 2019), binned to four classes (water/wetlands, developed, forested, barren/shrubs, crops-including-pasture); the stream network came from the Iowa DNR. ACTIONABLE FOR THIS PROJECT: the existing riparian test used a 0-2 km bucket and yielded CLF +0.039 PR-AUC with REG worse. This paper's signal is at 100 m — a 20x tighter band that a 2 km bucket would dilute by roughly its area ratio. Recomputing crop fraction in a 100 m (or 100-500 m) stream buffer, using the same 30 m CDL/NLCD grid already in the pipeline plus an NHDPlus flowline layer the project already has via COMID, is a cheap, purely-static, between-site feature requiring no new data acquisition and no gauge. CAVEATS: R^2 = 0.94 is fitted on FIVE nested watersheds in-sample with no validation split, so it is a direction not an expected effect size; the relation was established for SUMMER BASEFLOW LOAD specifically, which is the LOW-concentration, low-load regime (baseflow was <= 15% of annual load in every watershed), not the spring stormflow regime that carried 37.5 +/- 11.5% of annual load and produced the maximum concentrations that drive violation flags.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Summer baseflow NO3 load vs % cropped area within 100 m of stream: R^2 = 0.94, p < 0.01. Drainage structures vs number of cropped areas: R^2 = 0.95, p < 0.01. Baseflow was <=15% of annual load; spring stormflow 37.5 +/- 11.5% of annual load
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 5 (nested)

tier3_unverified.claim: THE DECISIVE NEGATIVE FOR THIS PROJECT: Valayamkunnath, Gochis, Chen, Barlage & Franz (2022), 'Modeling the Hydrologic Influence of Subsurface Tile Drainage Using the National Water Model', Water Resources Research 58(4), DOI 10.1029/2021WR031242, states that the NWM — a 1-km distributed model forecasting 2.7 million U.S. reaches — 'currently lacks tile drainage representation, creating considerable uncertainty in areas with extensive drainage systems.' Adding a tile-drainage scheme produced 20-50% accuracy improvements, and increased simulated streamflow peaks by 14%, volume by 2.3%, and baseflow by 11%. This is EXACTLY the failure mode that matters here: the project already identifies tile drainage as 'the dominant hydrologic control in Iowa' and absent from its features. NWM retrospective discharge in Iowa is therefore biased by the SAME missing process the project is trying to proxy, and the bias is SPATIALLY STRUCTURED by drainage density — i.e. it is a between-site error, precisely the term where all remaining headroom lies. Modeled-Q error could swamp the signal. Note the abstract was obtained via OpenAlex; the Wiley full text returned HTTP 403.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: 20-50% accuracy improvement from adding tile drainage; peaks +14%, volume +2.3%, baseflow +11%
tier3_unverified.nBasins: unknown (regional Midwest tile-drained domain; per-basin count not determinable from abstract — full text paywalled/403)

tier3_unverified.claim: ON THE C-Q REGIME QUESTION (LOWER-CONFIDENCE — from search-result summaries, not primary full-text fetches; treat as leads to verify, not as established figures): the nitrate C-Q literature uses the ratio of coefficients of variation CVc/CVq as the chemostasis metric, with Thompson et al. (2011, WRR, DOI 10.1029/2010WR009605) proposing CVc/CVq < 0.3 as the chemostatic threshold, and Basu et al. reporting that 'chemostatic behavior and constant CVc/CVq values below 0.5 are typical for agriculturally influenced catchments', arising 'when a large mass store buffers concentration variability' (i.e. legacy N). STRATEGIC IMPLICATION IF TRUE, AND IT CUTS AGAINST THE DISCHARGE ANGLE: chemostasis means nitrate CONCENTRATION is approximately INVARIANT to discharge in exactly this catchment class, so knowing Q at an ungauged Iowa site would add little direct information about concentration — the between-site level would instead be set by the N mass store (legacy N, tile density), NOT by Q. This is CONSISTENT with the project's own seven failed temporal/hydrologic ablations and with the finding that gains came only from static geography. It also argues the reverse of the LOAD-target proposal: under chemostasis L = C x Q is dominated by Q, so modeling load then back-dividing by a BIASED modeled Q would inject NWM's tile-drainage bias directly into the recovered concentration. I could NOT verify the primary Basu et al. (2010) and Thompson et al. (2011) numbers, sample sizes, or catchment counts within this fetch.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: CVc/CVq < 0.3 = chemostatic threshold (Thompson 2011); CVc/CVq < 0.5 typical of agricultural catchments (Basu)
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: not-applicable (descriptive C-Q regime classification, no predictive split)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: unknown (catchment counts for Basu et al. 2010 and Thompson et al. 2011 not determinable from secondary summaries)

Outputs are available in NetCDF and, notably, in **Zarr on AWS**, and the authors state they "downloaded [data] based on the NWM forecast point reference number" (feature_id / NHDPlusV2 COMID) and processed locally. This confirms the exact access mechanism our project would use: cloud Zarr on S3, joined per-reach by COMID, which we already store per basin. CAVEAT: this is v2.1, NOT v3.0; the retrospective ends 2020 while our nitrate record runs to 2026, so NWM v2.1 alone cannot cover 2021-2026 (v3.0 extends to ~2023 and would need separate verification).

tier3_unverified.claim: Across **3260 USGS gauges (548 natural-flow, 2712 regulated-flow)**, only **57% of natural-flow points had KGE > 0.5** and only **43% of regulated-flow points had KGE > 0.5** for hourly NWM v2.1 retrospective streamflow. On percent bias, **only 50% of natural-flow points and 36% of regulated-flow points fell within ±10% PBIAS**. The authors conclude "bias correction is crucial for utilizing the NWM retrospective streamflow dataset." DIRECT IMPLICATION FOR OUR PROJECT: at a randomly chosen ungauged Iowa pin there is roughly a coin-flip chance that NWM Q is off by more than 10% in the mean, and roughly a 43-57% chance KGE ≤ 0.5. Since our proposed use is a BETWEEN-SITE dilution/specific-discharge denominator, a per-site multiplicative bias of this magnitude propagates directly into the between-site concentration term — the exact term where our headroom lies. Bias correction is not available at an ungauged pin (it requires local observed Q), so we would have to accept the raw biased Q.

For **North Central RFC (NCRFC, humid, 55 natural-flow + 362 regulated-flow gauges, median NF drainage area 916.8 km2)**, natural-flow median PBIAS was **−10.15% (Q1 −20.21, Q3 +2.19) for sub-watersheds (10,000–50,000 ha = 100–500 km2)** and **−3.08% (Q1 −9.09, Q3 +6.62) for watersheds (>50,000 ha)** — i.e., systematic UNDER-estimation of flow, worst at the smaller basin sizes that dominate our 85 sites. For **Missouri Basin RFC (MBRFC, semi-arid, covers western Iowa, 58 NF + 269 RF gauges)**, natural-flow median PBIAS was **+4.46% (milli-watersheds), +5.93% (sub-watersheds), +11.02% (watersheds)** — systematic OVER-estimation. This is a falsifiable, directly usable prediction: NWM Q in Iowa should be biased low in the Mississippi-draining east and biased high in the Missouri-draining west, with a swing of order 15-20 percentage points across the state. That is a spatially structured error that would inject a spurious east-west gradient into any C = Load/Q or dilution feature — and our model's top features already include lon and lat, so a west-east artifact is the worst possible failure mode here.

The authors attribute regulated-flow failure to "natural and anthropogenic alterations in the drainage basin environment that may not be accurately captured by the model due to **static inputs such as land use/cover and catchment topography**." RELEVANCE: many Iowa stream reaches are hydrologically altered (channelization, tile drainage, impoundments) and would be classified as regulated or at least non-natural; small headwater basins are exactly where an arbitrary map pin is most likely to land. A ~47% median flow bias at 10–100 km2 basins would make a modeled-Q dilution denominator worse than useless at the small end of the deployment range.

tier3_unverified.claim: NEGATIVE-RESULT / SCOPE GAP: the paper's 25 pages of error attribution discuss forcing-data bias, model structure, parameters, snowpack, aridity, regulation, and static land-cover inputs — but contain **NO assessment whatsoever of artificial subsurface (tile) drainage**, and no evaluation stratified by drainage-class, soil, or low-relief agricultural terrain. The paper's only relevant structural statement is that regulated-flow error arises because "static inputs such as land use/cover and catchment topography" do not capture basin alterations. Therefore the specific bias we most need to know about — NWM v2.1 skill in tile-drained, low-relief Iowa catchments where subsurface drainage rather than surface runoff dominates the hydrograph — **is not answered by this source and must be sourced elsewhere** (candidates: the HESS benchmarking paper Johnson et al. 2023, hess.copernicus.org/articles/27/1809/2023, and the USGS ScienceBase NWM v2.1 daily benchmark dataset at sciencebase.gov/catalog/item/62336af9d34ec9f19eeb48fd, which publishes per-gauge NSE/KGE and would let us compute the Iowa-specific distribution ourselves at our 22 gauged sites). Do NOT treat this paper's CONUS-level 'humid regions perform best' finding as evidence that NWM works in tile-drained Iowa; NWM's WRF-Hydro/Noah-MP core has no tile-drainage parameterization at all.

tier3_unverified.claim: Seasonality of NWM bias is large and misaligned with the Iowa nitrate season. In **humid regions** (which includes NCRFC/eastern Iowa) NWM natural-flow median PBIAS is closest to zero in **winter** — described as "the model's best performance" — while "the model tends to **underestimate streamflow during the spring season**, which could be attributed to the model's limitations in snowmelt-dominated regions." In arid regions the median PBIAS ran **+7.85% (fall), +18.80% (winter), +19.54% (spring), +11.89% (summer)**. CRITICAL FOR US: Iowa nitrate violations concentrate in the **spring–early summer flush (roughly April–June)**, precisely the season the paper flags as NWM's weakest in humid/snow-influenced regions. A dilution feature C ∝ Load/Q built on NWM Q would therefore be least trustworthy exactly during the event window our classifier is supposed to call. This yields a concrete, cheap falsification test we can run before investing: at our **22 gauged sites (0.66–0.97 density, up to 18 years)**, pull NWM v2.1 retrospective Q by COMID and compute per-site KGE and monthly PBIAS against observed Q; if spring PBIAS is large and site-varying, modeled Q cannot supply between-site skill and the whole C-Q avenue should be abandoned or restricted to the 22 gauged sites only.

(2024, WRR, doi:10.1029/2023WR036591) modeled the backward-looking 7-day-average nitrate CONCENTRATION at 46 predominantly agricultural stream sites in the midwestern and eastern US using LSTMs whose DAILY INPUTS INCLUDE OBSERVED DISCHARGE plus meteorological time series, alongside static watershed attributes (anthropogenic hydrologic modification, N application, climate, groundwater, land use/land cover, watershed physical attributes, soils). Because observed daily Q is a required dynamic input and every one of the four modeling schemes trained on data FROM the sites being predicted, this design is NOT a prediction-in-ungauged-basins design and is not directly transferable to an arbitrary Iowa map pin with no gauge and no nitrate history; adopting its architecture would require substituting a MODELED Q (e.g. NWM retrospective) whose error at that site is unquantified by this paper. FALSIFIABLE: the paper contains no experiment in which a site is entirely withheld from training.

If terrane encoding beats lat/lon, the between-site deficit is a missing-geology problem; if it does not, lat/lon is capturing something else.

tier3_unverified.claim: Discharge alone is a weak predictor of nitrate concentration WITHIN a site: across the 275 German catchments with paired C and Q data, the log-log power-law C-Q regression for NO3-N had a mean R2 of only 0.27 ± 0.24 (Ebeling et al. 2021, Section 3.1). I independently downloaded the paper's own CC-BY dataset (WQQDB, HydroShare doi:10.4211/hs.9b4deeca259b4f7398ce72121b4e2979, CQ_metrics.csv) and recomputed over the 274 independent catchments with a valid nitrate slope: median C-Q R2 = 0.223, quartiles 0.044 / 0.223 / 0.458, and only 39.4% of catchments exceed R2 = 0.30. DIRECT IMPLICATION FOR THE DEPLOYMENT TARGET: even a PERFECT, error-free discharge time series at an ungauged pin would explain a median of ~22% of log-nitrate variance at that site; a modeled Q (NWM retrospective) carrying its own error can only do worse. This bounds the upside of the whole modeled-discharge angle and says it cannot be the fix for the between-site level problem.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: mean C-Q power-law R2 = 0.27 ± 0.24; median 0.223 (IQR 0.044-0.458); 39.4% of catchments > 0.30
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 275 (274 independent) German catchments with paired C-Q; 2000-2015

tier3_unverified.claim: Nitrate in these catchments shows ENRICHMENT (mobilization), not dilution: mean C-Q log-log slope b = 0.26 ± 0.35 (median ± IQR 0.16 ± 0.36) for NO3-N, versus b = -0.22 ± 0.27 for phosphate. 69% of catchments (n=188) were classified as enrichment patterns and 74% (n=200) as a chemostatic regime (CVc/CVq = 0.47 ± 0.43, median 0.33). My recomputation on the 274 independent catchments: 82.1% have b > 0; only 5.8% (16 catchments) have b <= -0.1, i.e. genuine dilution; 36.1% fall in |b| < 0.1 and 58.0% in b > 0.1; 90.1% have CVc/CVq < 1. FALSIFIES the dilution-mass-balance framing for the fluid-dynamics angle: a C = Load/Q model (C decreasing with Q) is the WRONG sign for agricultural nitrate in ~82% of catchments. It also means concentration varies far less than discharge, so the site's absolute LEVEL is set by source strength, not by flow — consistent with this project's finding that the deficit is between-site static information.

tier3_unverified.claim: MEAN nitrate concentration is highly predictable BETWEEN unmonitored catchments from static attributes alone, with no discharge and no local nitrate history: random forest reached R2_crossval = 0.69 (R2_OOB = 0.68) and PLS regression R2_crossval = 0.64 (R2_train = 0.66) for mean NO3-N over n = 759 catchments. Protocol: 3-times-repeated 10-fold cross-validation where each unit is a whole catchment, so every test catchment's concentrations are entirely unseen (the ungauged-basin analogue) — BUT folds are random rather than spatially blocked, so a held-out catchment can have a geographic neighbour in training; this makes 0.69 an optimistic upper bound relative to a leave-one-region-out protocol. Top RF importances: f_forest 20.3, mean annual precipitation P_mm 17.4, precipitation seasonality P_SIsw 16.2, fraction sedimentary aquifer f_sedim 15.8, vertical concentration heterogeneity het_v 14.4, f_agric 13.9. SAMPLE-SIZE FLAG: n=759 catchments versus this project's 19 independent basin families — a 40x difference. A 40-predictor RF fit on 19 units cannot reproduce this; the transferable lesson is WHICH variable classes carry the between-site signal (land-cover fractions, precipitation climatology, aquifer/subsurface type), not the R2 value.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: RF R2_crossval = 0.69 (OOB 0.68); PLSR R2_crossval = 0.64 (train 0.66)

tier3_unverified.claim: NITROGEN SURPLUS WAS A WEAKER BETWEEN-SITE PREDICTOR OF MEAN NITRATE THAN PLAIN LAND-COVER FRACTION. Forest fraction alone explained 32% and agricultural fraction alone 29% of the between-catchment variance in mean NO3-N in simple linear regression (n=759), while the correlation of mean NO3-N with N surplus was only r = 0.39 for N_surp_80 (1980-2015 legacy-inclusive surplus), i.e. r2 ~ 0.15 — despite N surplus being strongly correlated with agricultural land (r = 0.71). The authors attribute the gap to 'a few catchments that have exceptionally high N surplus but moderate mean NO3-N concentrations', and note the agriculture-to-nitrate relationship is 'highly heteroscedastic', with deviations explained by soil and aquifer properties (denitrification buffering; f_sedim ranked high). N surplus does NOT appear in the top six predictors of mean NO3-N in either the PLSR or the RF model. FALSIFIES the proposed between-site relation 'concentration ~ N-input-yield / specific-discharge' as a strong predictor, and independently corroborates this project's negative result on broadcasting 2017 N-surplus forward: the surplus product may be the wrong variable, not merely the wrong vintage. Practical read: crop/land-cover fractions plus subsurface attributes beat an N-budget product.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: f_forest alone R2 = 0.32; f_agric alone R2 = 0.29; N_surp_80 correlation r = 0.39 (r2 ~ 0.15); all descriptors together 0.64-0.70
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 759 German catchments

tier3_unverified.claim: NEGATIVE RESULT ON DISCHARGE-DERIVED FEATURES FOR NITRATE SPECIFICALLY: the study computed a full suite of hydrological descriptors (mean discharge, mean SPECIFIC discharge, runoff coefficient, seasonal ratio, base-flow index, flashiness index) and ran a supplementary analysis adding them. These descriptors 'substantially increased the variance explained ... between 11% and 37%' for TOC on a subset of n = 184 catchments (raising RF slope-b from R2_crossval = 0.28 to 0.44, and PLSR CVc/CVq to 0.58). For NITRATE, no such improvement is reported anywhere in the paper, and not a single hydrological descriptor appears in the top six of ANY of the four NO3-N models (mean concentration, slope b, CVc/CVq — PLSR and RF); the NO3-N models are instead topped by land cover, precipitation climatology, subsurface/aquifer type, topographic slope and TWI. DIRECT ANSWER TO THE RESEARCH QUESTION: in the largest study of its kind, adding real (gauged, not modeled) discharge statistics measurably helped organic carbon but did NOT surface as a control on nitrate level or nitrate C-Q behaviour. This argues that acquiring modeled Q (NWM v3 retrospective) for the ungauged pin is unlikely to convert into between-site nitrate skill, and should be ranked below static subsurface/land-cover attributes. Caveat: absence of reporting for NO3 is weaker evidence than an explicit stated null, and these are OBSERVED gauge discharges, so this does not separately test modeled-Q bias in tile-drained basins — a question this German-catchment paper does not address at all (tile-drainage density is not among its predictors; 'drain_dens' is stream drainage density, not artificial subsurface drainage).

tier3_unverified.claim: THE CHEMOSTASIS HYPOTHESIS FOR AGRICULTURAL CATCHMENTS (Basu et al. 2010; Thompson et al. 2011) IS EXPLICITLY CONTRADICTED AT SCALE. Among agriculturally dominated catchments (f_agric >= 0.5), 34% exhibited CHEMODYNAMIC export regimes — of which 89% were combined with enrichment patterns — compared with only 17% chemodynamic among less-agricultural catchments (f_agric < 0.5). Higher agricultural fraction was associated with HIGHER slope b and HIGHER CVc/CVq, the opposite of the homogenization/chemostasis expectation. The authors state directly: 'Our study therefore does not support the generality of the hypothesis that highly managed, agricultural catchments are necessarily subject to homogenization of sources and thus to chemostatic export regimes (Basu et al., 2010; Thompson et al., 2011).' They attribute the chemodynamic behaviour to vertical concentration heterogeneity (het_v) from subsurface denitrification producing a depth decline in nitrate — high flow taps shallow, N-rich water. CONSEQUENCE FOR THIS PROJECT: (a) do not assume a fixed chemostatic C-Q form for Iowa row-crop basins as a modeling prior; (b) the abstract also states that mean NO3 concentrations AND THEIR VARIANCE AMONG SITES both increase with agricultural land use — heteroscedasticity means the highest-agriculture Iowa basins are precisely the hardest to place on an absolute level, which is exactly the failure mode reported here (between_r2 0.21); (c) the mechanism identified (vertical redox/denitrification contrast between shallow seepage and groundwater) is a STATIC subsurface attribute, obtainable without any local sensor, and is the single most important predictor of nitrate C-Q dynamics (het_v ranked first in 3 of 4 dynamics models) — a candidate feature class this project has not tried.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: 34% of f_agric>=0.5 catchments chemodynamic (89% of those with enrichment) vs 17% for f_agric<0.5
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 274-759 German catchments (agricultural subset f_agric >= 0.5 within these)
